rule: Full run. Questions chosen from per-domain slices by Opus 5.5 proposers before any grading; key points only from accepted / score >= 10 answers, each citing its answer id (extract cuts answers at ~2,000 chars). intended_domains is the coverage plan, not a label.

questions.query: How does a hash table work?

key_points.text: A hash function maps the key to an integer, which is reduced (e.g. hash % number_of_buckets) to an index into an array of buckets; lookup recomputes the hash and inspects only that bucket.

Collisions are unavoidable because the key space is larger than the index space; they are commonly handled by keeping a list (chain) of entries per bucket and comparing the full key against each entry.
Tables resize (allocate a bigger bucket array and rehash entries) to keep the load factor, the ratio of elements to buckets, roughly in the 0.5-1.0 / ~70% range.
With a good hash function and bounded load factor the average chain length stays constant regardless of table size, which is why lookup/insert/erase are O(1).

Separate chaining is not the only scheme: open addressing (closed hashing) stores entries in the array itself, but has less stable performance with collision-prone keys/hash functions and with erasure.
A good general-purpose hash function scatters keys effectively at random (similar keys get dissimilar hashes); identity/weak hashes are fast but collision-prone in the worst case.

questions.query: Why doesn't Dijkstra's algorithm work for negative weight edges?

key_points.text: Once Dijkstra extracts/closes a vertex it treats its distance as final and never revisits it; with a negative edge a later path through a not-yet-closed vertex can be shorter, so the result is wrong.
The correctness argument relies on non-negative weights: adding a non-negative edge can never make a path shorter, so the minimum-distance vertex in the open set already has its shortest distance.
Small counterexample: edges A->C (2), A->B (5), B->C (-10); Dijkstra closes C at 2 and misses A->B->C = -5.
Bellman-Ford handles negative edges by 'looking back' (a DP-style relaxation of all edges) at higher cost; the non-negativity assumption is what lets Dijkstra run faster (O(E log V)).
Dijkstra cannot detect negative cycles; if a negative cycle is reachable from the source no shortest path exists and its output is necessarily wrong.

questions.query: How can I pair socks from a pile efficiently?

key_points.text: Sorting is more than needed: pairing only requires equality groups, not an order, so hashing/partitioning is enough and faster than an O(N log N) sort.

Recursive hash partitioning (piles by colour, then by pattern, until piles are small) is the same technique databases such as SQL Server use for hash joins and hash aggregates over huge inputs, and it scales linearly.
Like the element distinctness problem, the task is solvable in O(N) with a single hash distribution on all attributes, which is optimal since every sock must be examined.

Parallel workers sharing piles suffer synchronization costs (Universal Scalability Law); it scales when each worker has its own piles and the pile sets are merged at the end (e.g. via an aggregation tree).
The naive approach of comparing each new sock against all unmatched ones is O(n^2) in the worst case when only equality comparison is available; sorting brings it to N log N.

questions.query: Why is the knapsack problem pseudo-polynomial?

key_points.text: The DP runs in O(nW), but W is written in only log W bits, so the running time is exponential in the input length (O(n * 2^bits(W))); polynomial in the numeric value but not in the input size is what pseudo-polynomial means.
Complexity is measured against the size of the input encoding (number of bits), not the magnitude of the values; adding one bit to W doubles the running time.
Naive primality testing by trial division up to sqrt(n) is another example: its step count depends on the magnitude n, so it is exponential in the number of bits of n.
Most algorithms do not show this because numbers fit in fixed-size machine words handled at constant cost; knapsack is unusually sensitive to the magnitude of the parameter W.
By contrast, linear search over an array of n elements is genuinely polynomial because n there is the length of the input, not a number inside it.

questions.query: Why does the integrality gap of an LP relaxation matter for approximation algorithms?

key_points.text: The integrality gap of a relaxation bounds what any approximation algorithm based on that relaxation can achieve: if the gap is x, such an algorithm cannot guarantee better than an x-approximation.

Rounding analyses compare the algorithm's solution to the relaxation's optimum (e.g. prove V >= OPT(LP)/c) because OPT(IP) is unknown; when the gap exceeds c such a guarantee is impossible in general.
The integrality gap is a property of a particular relaxation/formulation, separate from the rounding procedure; a gap of c tells you a different formulation is needed to prove a ratio better than c.

For many problems the integrality gap of a natural LP/SDP equals both the best known approximation ratio and the hardness ratio; assuming the Unique Games Conjecture, for CSPs the optimal approximation ratio equals the integrality gap of a simple SDP (Raghavendra).
Integrality gaps are unconditional lower bounds for restricted models of computation: being geometric rather than computational, they need no assumption such as P != NP.
Rounding algorithms are used to produce an actual near-optimal integral solution (not just approximate the optimal value) and are often how an upper bound on the integrality gap is proved.

questions.query: Why is char[] preferred over String for passwords?

key_points.text: Java Strings are immutable, so a password held in a String cannot be overwritten or zeroed and stays in memory until garbage collection; a char[] can be explicitly wiped as soon as it is no longer needed.

Using char[] only narrows the window for memory-dump style attacks: the array holds the password while in use, the GC may leave stray copies when moving it, and the realistic exposure is via core dumps or swap.
A String password is more easily leaked by accidentally printing or logging it; printing a char[] shows only the array reference.

Official guidance (Java Cryptography Architecture guide, Java Secure Coding Guidelines) says to collect and store security-sensitive data in char arrays, clear them after use, and not log sensitive data, while noting clearing is less effective because the runtime moves objects.
Strings may be interned and kept alive in the constant pool, which char[] avoids.

questions.query: PUT vs PATCH in REST APIs: what is the real difference and why is PATCH not idempotent?

key_points.text: PUT sends a complete representation of the entity that replaces whatever is stored at the URI, while PATCH sends only the fields/changes to apply and leaves the rest of the resource untouched.
Because a PUT carries the entire entity, repeating the same PUT always yields the same stored state, which is why PUT is idempotent.
Sending a partial entity with PUT replaces the resource with only the supplied fields, so omitted fields are dropped or set to null (data loss).

Idempotence means f(f(x)) = f(x); PATCH is not guaranteed idempotent because a patch document may contain operations (e.g. 'add' to a collection) that change the resource again each time it is applied.

PATCH can be designed to be idempotent (RFC 5789 notes this helps avoid collisions between concurrent patches): replace/add/delete-field operations stay idempotent, while operations like increment or append do not.
A PATCH body is a patch document: a set of instructions in some patch language (e.g. op/path/value) describing how to modify the resource, rather than a modified version of the resource itself.

questions.query: Differences between webhook and websocket

key_points.text: Webhooks are for server-to-server communication: one server registers a URL with another, which sends data to that URL when an event happens.

WebSockets are usually for server-to-browser communication: the client opens a persistent connection to a websocket server, which is faster and less resource-hungry than older long-polling/COMET approaches.

Both address real-time communication but solve different aspects; for a third-party API, webhooks leave the third party to push changes on to its browsers, whereas a websocket API lets end users connect directly.
Browser apps cannot receive webhooks, and websockets let a server app receive events without exposing a public URL or opening its firewall.
Webhooks suit apps with many subscriptions (no open connections to hold) and serverless functions or sleeping hosts, which cannot keep a websocket connection open.

questions.query: Why were required and optional removed in Protocol Buffers 3?

key_points.text: A required field can never be safely added to or removed from a schema already in use: data or senders built with the old definition lack the field, so parsing/validation fails and wire compatibility breaks.
The point of protobuf is that fields can be added and removed while staying forward and backward compatible across newer and older binaries; required fields violate those compatibility semantics.
Upgrading every application first is error-prone and does not help when protos are persisted in a datastore, even a short-lived one like memcached.
Fields that look obviously required (e.g. an id) later need to change type (int32 to int64, int to string), leaving an obsolete required field that must still be set but is ignored.
Adding/removing required fields caused repeated production incidents at Google, where it is effectively banned; with required gone, optional became redundant and was removed too.

Opponents favored doing such checks in a more expressive validation layer with a better failure model; removal also fit proto3's simplicity alongside dropping field presence for primitives and custom defaults.

questions.query: SOAP vs REST: what are the differences?

key_points.text: REST is an architectural style, not a protocol; SOAP is a protocol defining an XML-based message format.

REST's defining constraints are client-server, statelessness (each request carries all its state), cacheability, and a uniform interface (standard HTTP methods on resources); the downside is being stuck with that interface.
SOAP is operation/action oriented (a URL maps to a function, essentially RPC), whereas REST is resource oriented (a URL identifies a thing and HTTP verbs act on it).
SOAP supports only XML wrapped in an envelope but can run over almost any transport; REST allows several formats such as JSON (smaller payloads) and relies on HTTP.

SOAP's WS-* standards add enterprise features: WS-Security for end-to-end message-level security beyond transport TLS, WS-AtomicTransaction for ACID/two-phase commit, WS-ReliableMessaging; REST relies on transport security and client retries.
REST reads can be cached and REST needs less bandwidth and is simpler; SOAP reads cannot use web caching and SOAP is slower and heavier.
SOAP defines an explicit contract in WSDL, so clients need prior knowledge of operations and types; REST clients should need nothing beyond hypermedia.

questions.query: REST vs gRPC: when should I choose one over the other?

key_points.text: Done correctly, REST improves long-term evolvability and scalability at the cost of performance and complexity; it suits services developed and maintained independently, like the Web, where client and server are loosely coupled.
RPC services can be simpler and faster at the cost of flexibility and independence; they suit cases where client and server are tightly coupled and share a development cycle.
Most so-called REST APIs are not RESTful but tightly coupled RPC in disguise, so a standardized RPC framework implemented properly may serve better.
REST's promise is a uniform interface letting generic clients use resources that did not exist when they were written, an ideal realized mainly for the human-readable Web.
Semantically correct HTTP carries method, URL, status and Cache-Control/Vary, so a transparent caching layer comes nearly free with REST, while gRPC must roll its own caching.
gRPC brings efficient protobuf encoding, HTTP/2 multiplexing and header compression, generated clients from a declared interface in many languages, and full-duplex streaming.

questions.query: What is the difference between CurrentCulture and CurrentUICulture in .NET CultureInfo?

key_points.text: CurrentCulture represents the user's default locale/regional settings and controls default formatting of numbers, dates and currency (e.g. ToString).
CurrentUICulture represents the user-interface language and drives UI localization/translation: the ResourceManager uses it to pick localized resources (e.g. a .fr-CA.resx file).
The two are often the same but can differ, e.g. German number/date formats with an English UI.
In ASP.NET, CurrentCulture defaults to the web server's setup, while CurrentUICulture can be taken from the client's user agent so localized strings follow the visitor's language.
CurrentUICulture accepts neutral cultures such as 'en', whereas CurrentCulture requires a specific culture such as 'en-GB'; setting it to a neutral culture throws ArgumentException.

questions.query: How does Google PageSpeed lossless image compression work for PNG and JPEG?

key_points.text: For PNG, PageSpeed tries several combinations of PNG filter setting and zlib compression strategy (like OptiPNG -o2..-o7) and keeps the smallest result.

For JPEG, the lossless gain comes from re-encoding with jpeglib without changing pixels: dropping EXIF data and color profiles and optimizing the Huffman tables (jpegtran -optimize reproduces PageSpeed's sizes exactly).
The underlying principle is trading encoder CPU time for compression: compression is a search for shorter representations, and tools like Photoshop do not search hard.
Savings also come from using format capabilities fully, e.g. PNG8+alpha instead of PNG24+alpha, or optimized Huffman tables in JPEG.
The same results can be had with jpegoptim --strip-all for JPEG and optipng for PNG; higher optimization levels take longer to run.
PageSpeed can also losslessly convert an image to whichever format is smallest (image_converter), and compresses WebP losslessly with libwebp.

questions.query: Why does the US government disallow dynamic languages for secure projects?

key_points.text: Dynamic-language features such as Ruby open classes (or Perl tie) let code anywhere silently redefine core behaviour, e.g. make every String write to a file or the network, hidden from auditors.
Because of such runtime dynamism, many static security-analysis approaches do not work; even parsing Perl is undecidable.
Security scanners handle dynamic behaviours badly and produce many false positives, so organisations that rely on those tools without manual-review capacity end up treating such code as insecure.
Military, aviation and heavy industry systems have terrible failure modes, so they impose strict rules on languages and compilers, and security policy is written for the worst case.
Dynamism itself is not necessarily the issue: interpreters must be approved and installed on target systems, which requires source analysis, compiling, binary analysis and conflict checks.
Safety-critical systems such as the F-16 and Boeing 777 use Ada because strong static typing and compile-time checks catch errors that other languages only reveal at run time.
Dynamic languages can 'swallow' bugs into unexpected behaviour, which is dangerous in sensitive systems where you want failures to surface as early as possible.

questions.query: I found my company is putting a backdoor into mobile phones; what should I do?

key_points.text: 'We are not going to use it' is irrelevant: a backdoor is a built-in vulnerability that anyone who finds it can exploit.
Frame it for management as business risk: ask 'what happens to us when somebody finds and publishes this?', because the fix cost and reputation damage would be severe.

If decision-makers are informed and still ship it, the company is knowingly shipping a serious vulnerability; consider reporting to the authorities and talk to a lawyer about protection from retaliation.
A security analyst's role is to identify and communicate risk in the proper forum; accepting the risk is the business's decision, and your own option is whether to keep working there.
Protect yourself if you escalate: consider anonymous whistleblowing or written notice to corporate counsel, or report it as a vulnerability (e.g. CVE).
The liability is comparable to Sony's rootkit fiasco, whose cost in money and reputation reached hundreds of millions of dollars.

questions.query: Are quantum computers just a variant of analog computers?

key_points.text: Analog computers cannot pass Bell tests; quantum computers can.
An analog computer with N sliders has an N-dimensional state space, while N qubits have a 2^N-dimensional state space.
Error-correcting an analog computer turns it into a digital computer, whereas a quantum computer remains quantum after error correction.
Analog computers are not sensitive to decoherence and do not break if data is accidentally copied; quantum computations do break.
Analog computers cannot efficiently run Shor's, Grover's or other quantum algorithms.

questions.query: How does the reparameterization trick for VAEs work and why is it important?

key_points.text: Backpropagation cannot flow through a random sampling node; the reparameterization trick moves the randomness into an independent noise variable so gradients flow through deterministic nodes to the encoder parameters.

The sample is rewritten as a deterministic function of the parameters and parameter-free noise (e.g. z = mu + sigma*epsilon, epsilon ~ N(0,1)), so the expectation is taken over a distribution that no longer depends on the parameters and the gradient can move inside it.
The alternative score-function (log-derivative / REINFORCE-style) estimator E[f * grad log q] is unbiased but typically has high variance; the reparameterized estimator has lower variance.
The trick only applies when q can be expressed as a deterministic transformation g(epsilon, x) of noise from a simple distribution; this is not always possible but holds for many useful classes of q.
The score-function estimate is poor because essential contributions can come from rare x values where q is small, which a finite sample may never hit (an importance-sampling view).

questions.query: Generative vs. discriminative models: what is the difference and when are generative models useful?

key_points.text: Discriminative models learn the (hard or soft) boundary between classes, while generative models model the distribution of the individual classes.

SVMs and decision trees count as discriminative because they learn explicit boundaries or splits without a model of how points are generated; discriminative effectively covers any classifier that is not generative.
A generative model gives P(X|Y) and P(Y), so P(Y|X) can be obtained via Bayes' theorem; discriminative models do not have the reverse (generative) property.

Generative algorithms impose structural assumptions on the data (e.g. Naive Bayes' conditional independence of features), whereas their discriminative counterparts such as logistic regression make fewer assumptions.

Generative models make it easier to detect and adapt to distribution change (non-stationary data, unsupervised online updates) and generally support outlier detection, which discriminative models generally do not.
Gaussian mixture models vs k-means illustrate the contrast: the GMM is a probabilistic model of how points are generated, k-means is not.

questions.query: Why not prune your neural network?

key_points.text: Pruning only increases efficiency after training is done; you still have to train the full-size network first.

Most compute over a model's life goes to development (training many times, architecture and hyperparameter search), so savings on the deployed network are a drop in the bucket, and researchers focus on training rather than deployment.
A pruned network may not be faster: frameworks are optimized for dense matrix multiplication and cannot exploit weights set to zero, so the result is smaller but often no faster.
Pruning can yield speedups if a very large fraction of weights is removed (so sparse multiplication wins), if pruning is structured at channel level, or with specialized hardware or frameworks.
The lottery ticket hypothesis (Frankle & Carbin) suggests a large network contains a good subnetwork that training finds, which is why you need to train the large network to prune it.

questions.query: What is the purpose of the [CLS] token in BERT and why is its encoder output used for classification?

key_points.text: [CLS] stands for classification; it was introduced so BERT has a sentence-level representation (pooling) to use for classification.
No ordinary input word's output can be used because each such output is that word's representation, so a dedicated token with no other purpose serves as the sentence representation.
BERT is pretrained on masked language modeling and next sentence prediction; the [CLS] output is what is used to predict whether the second sentence follows the first.

[CLS] itself has a fixed embedding and position and carries no information, but its output is computed from all other words through the encoder, so it aggregates the sentence; an averaged token vector is an alternative.

questions.query: Fast algorithm to compare images and detect exact or near duplicates

key_points.text: Keypoint matching picks informative points (edges, corners) rather than random ones; SIFT keypoints match images across scale, rotation and lighting changes.
Naive keypoint matching is slow (O(n^2 m) over n keypoints and m database images); structures such as quadtrees or binary space partitioning can find the closest match faster.
A faster but less robust method builds normalized color and texture histograms per image and compares them by summing absolute bucket differences; it fails on rescaled, rotated or discolored images.
Simple keypoints combined with randomized decision trees (keypoint recognition with randomized trees, random ferns, BRIEF) are fast while keeping SIFT-like invariance.
A perceptual hash reduces each image to a compact fingerprint of salient features, giving far fewer false positives than comparing tiny thumbnails.

questions.query: Is it always better to use the whole dataset (including the test set) to train the final model?

key_points.text: A held-out test set only gives an estimate of future performance, not a guarantee; actual performance may be worse or better than estimated.

Standard practice is, after selecting the model and hyperparameters, to retrain on all available data for production; in expectation this is no worse than using part of the data and potentially better.
Once the model is retrained on all data, you can no longer make statistical claims about its accuracy on unseen data because no test set remains.
The workflow loops over training, validating and changing the model, and only at the end assesses performance once on the test set.
If true target values of new production data become known, they act like test data and allow real-time performance monitoring of the deployed model.

questions.query: Why do medical imaging works focus on reducing false positives when false negatives seem more dangerous?

key_points.text: Diseases are rare, so even with equal false positive and false negative rates the absolute number of false positives vastly exceeds false negatives (base rate effect).
Each false positive can lead to actively harmful, unnecessary treatment such as invasive surgery, chemotherapy or radiotherapy.
A tool that 'cries wolf' too often gets ignored or switched off by clinicians, so reducing the false positive rate is needed for physicians to use it.
When an assistive tool keeps flagging patients who are already in hospital, it effectively tells the physician nothing new.

questions.query: Why are LLMs able to reproduce bodies of known text exactly?

key_points.text: Famous texts appear many times on the web, so LLM training sets likely contain several copies of them, which explains exact reproduction.
Some LLM training datasets try to deduplicate their data.
Information-theoretically, LLMs are a very lossy compression of their training corpora, large enough that 'decompressing' parts is recognizable and reasonably faithful.
Models have also been found to reproduce exact or near-exact text for personal information that appears only once in the corpus, not only for very common material.
'The probable outcome given a prompt' assumes a probability model derived from the training corpus; a naive Markov chain shows how such text can be encoded reproducibly in that model.

questions.query: What is the advantage of keeping batch size a power of 2?

key_points.text: It is a matter of mapping virtual processors onto the GPU's physical processors; the number of physical processors is often a power of 2, so other counts lead to poor performance.

Because GPUs use SIMD data parallelism, work that spills past a multiple of the processor count (e.g. 17 jobs on 16 processors) runs in an extra pass in which one processor works while the others idle.
The effect has nothing to do with learning or the optimization algorithm; it is purely a programming/hardware issue.

questions.query: What is a non-interactive zero-knowledge proof (NIZK)?

key_points.text: In a non-interactive ZK proof the verifier's random challenges are replaced by a hash function computed over the prover's commitments (the Fiat-Shamir heuristic); the hash result is the challenge.

In an interactive ZK proof the prover first issues commitments and the verifier then issues challenges; this proves anything only if the verifier chooses challenges independently, without prior understanding with the prover.

Security comes from modelling the hash as a random oracle: the prover cannot predict its output before producing the commitments, and because the hash is deterministic the challenge cannot be changed without changing the earlier messages.
Once the protocol is run against the hash-based simulator, the transcript can be handed to anyone, who can check it and be convinced the proof is real.

Fiat-Shamir costs security: a cheating prover can retry different commitments until the hash output suits him, so reaching an error below 2^-80 needs an underlying error below 2^-160; it is a heuristic with no proof.

Alternatively NIZK can be achieved with a common reference string: a random string drawn from a distribution, available to all parties, that no party can influence; it may avoid doubling the security parameter but is harder to realize.

questions.query: Prevent double-spending in a decentralized digital currency without all transactions being public

key_points.text: Preventing double spending means giving currency to one party must make the owner unable to give the same currency to another, and there are only three known mechanisms: a central authority, a distributed secure device, or making some aspect of all transactions public.
With a central authority, every transfer needs the authority's approval and must be reported to it so it can refuse a second transfer of the same coins.

With a distributed secure device, coins are held in physically secure hardware that refuses to give them away twice; in practice a central authority is still needed to load devices and issue certificates proving a genuine device was involved.
Bitcoin chooses the public-record approach, which seems best for decentralized cryptographic currencies; no fourth approach is known.

Only enough information to prove ownership of the coins and that they were not transferred elsewhere needs to be public; Bitcoin leaks much more (such as the destination account) and a protocol could be designed to reveal less.

questions.query: Is secp256r1 more secure than secp256k1?

key_points.text: The two curves have comparable security; the main difference is that secp256k1 is a Koblitz curve, and Koblitz curves are a few bits weaker, which does not matter at 256 bits absent a breakthrough.

With no known weakness the best attack on both is Pollard's rho, with cost sqrt(pi*n/(2m)) where m is the order of the curve automorphism; secp256k1 has an extra efficiently computable automorphism giving order 6 instead of 2, so about 127.03 bits versus 127.83 bits for secp256r1.
secp256r1's parameters supposedly come from random numbers, but it is impossible to prove this, so it would have been easier to backdoor; secp256k1's parameters were chosen relatively rigidly.

The risks differ rather than one being more secure: secp256r1 could be backdoored, while Koblitz curves as a class could turn out weak in some currently unknown way, so the preference is somewhat subjective.

questions.query: Why does uint8 cost more gas than uint256 in Solidity?

key_points.text: The EVM works with 256-bit (32-byte) words and every operation is based on these units.
When data is smaller than a word, extra operations are needed to convert between 256 bits and 8 bits, which is why a lone uint8 costs more gas.
Inside a struct uint8 does cost less than a full uint because of tight packing.
Declaring same-size members next to each other (uints with uints, bytes with bytes) improves the tight packing further.
With newer compilers the single-variable difference is small, and with several small variables (e.g. five uint8 state variables) or arrays the smaller type is cheaper than the uint256 version.

questions.query: Difference between require and assert, and between revert and throw, in Solidity

key_points.text: Before Solidity 0.8.0, assert(false) compiled to the invalid opcode 0xfe, consuming all remaining gas and reverting all changes, while require(false) compiled to 0xfd, the REVERT opcode, which refunds the remaining gas.
require should be used to validate user inputs, return values from external contract calls and state conditions before state changes, typically at the beginning of a function.
assert is for internal errors and invariants: properly functioning code should never reach a failing assert, and if it does there is a bug in the contract.
If used properly, analysis tools (such as the SMTChecker) can evaluate a contract to find conditions and calls that reach a failing assert.
Since 0.8.0, internal errors such as assertion failures and division by zero use revert with a special error instead of the invalid opcode, so they no longer waste gas; assert is essentially a panic.
throw is deprecated in favour of revert; revert reverts changes and refunds unused gas and is used for business-logic error conditions, and require and revert are much the same in the EVM.

questions.query: Why doesn't GCC optimize a*a*a*a*a*a to (a*a*a)*(a*a*a)?

key_points.text: Floating-point arithmetic is not associative, so the compiler may not regroup a*a*a*a*a*a into (a*a*a)*(a*a*a) without changing results; for integers GCC does perform this regrouping.
GCC will do the regrouping for floating point when given -funsafe-math-optimizations (fast-math), but this reordering violates IEEE-754, which is why it requires the flag.

Signed integer multiplication can be reordered without special flags because the result is exact absent overflow and overflow is undefined behaviour; unsigned integers work modulo a power of two and can be reordered freely.

Under the C FP_CONTRACT pragma a compiler may contract an expression into a single operation with one rounding (e.g. fma or an internal power function); GCC assumes it ON by default and -ffp-contract=off disables it.

Library pow is crafted for minimal error, while a chain of multiplications accumulates more rounding error, so trading pow for multiplications (or vice versa) is an accuracy-versus-speed choice the compiler must be careful about.
The C standard (5.1.2.2.3/15; C++11 1.9/9) allows operators to be regrouped only if they are really associative/commutative.

questions.query: What exactly does the PHI instruction do and how to use it in LLVM

key_points.text: A phi node selects a value depending on which predecessor block control arrived from (e.g. value a if the previous block was block1, b if block2).
Phi nodes are needed because in SSA form every variable may be defined only once, so a value assigned on two different paths (if/else) must be merged by a phi rather than reassigned.
A short-circuit || compiles to a conditional branch; in the merge block a phi yields true when coming from the entry block and the right-hand operand's value when coming from the rhs block.
A front end need not emit phi nodes: it can use stack-allocated variables with loads and stores, and LLVM's optimization passes convert that code into SSA with phi nodes automatically.
SSA enables a variety of compiler optimizations and is the de-facto standard for intermediate code.

questions.query: Why shouldn't I use PyPy over CPython if PyPy is 6.3 times faster?

key_points.text: PyPy's support for CPython C extensions is limited and often slow, so many libraries (including parts of the standard library written in C) require CPython.
Because PyPy is a JIT compiler, its gains come from long run times and simple types; short-running scripts may not be faster, and pre-JIT speed can be worse than CPython.
The 6.3x figure is a geometric mean over PyPy's own benchmark set; it says nothing guaranteed about any particular program, and not even that PyPy runs every CPython program.
PyPy is not 100% compatible because it does not simulate CPython internals, and in many cases it consumes more memory than CPython; it can also be slower than CPython on some code.

CPython uses reference counting so objects are freed promptly and __del__ runs predictably; PyPy uses only garbage collection, so software relying on CPython's deallocation timing is not ready to migrate.
PyPy's Python-version support typically lags a few versions behind CPython, and switching requires retooling (inertia).

questions.query: Why doesn't C++ have a garbage collector?

key_points.text: The issue is predictability of performance: mark-and-sweep collectors stop the world, while reference counting adds overhead (atomic counts under multithreading) and needs cycle detection.
C++ manages resources through RAII, scoped object lifetimes and smart pointers such as shared_ptr, so modern C++ largely does not need (or want) a garbage collector.
Garbage collection is hard to reconcile with destructors: deterministic object lifetimes are lost and it is unclear what to do when a destructor throws during collection.

GC is almost impossible to specify in the standard's terms of observable behaviour; since C++ probably cannot use a copying (moving) collector, the heap fragments and allocation success cannot be guaranteed.
Stroustrup hoped for an optionally enabled collector in C++0x, but technical problems left only a specification of how such a collector integrates with the language.
Third-party garbage collectors for C++ exist (e.g. Hans Boehm's collector), and C++ can be used as a garbage-collected language where GC is suitable.
C++'s principle is that you do not pay for features you do not use, which mandatory GC would violate.

questions.query: How should I read type system notation?

key_points.text: Type systems for programming languages are syntactic systems: a set of rules operating on the (abstract) syntax of the language.
Comprehensive treatments begin by giving the grammar of all syntactic constructs the type system considers, using BNF notation.
In the simplest typed languages syntax is needed for exactly two things, expressions and types (e.g. boolean and integer literals, conditionals, arithmetic, comparisons; types Bool and Int).
By convention e stands for an expression and tau for a type; other presentations use t, T, sigma or other Greek letters for types.

questions.query: What does the processor do while waiting for a main memory fetch after L1 and L2 cache misses?

key_points.text: Out-of-order/speculative execution keeps running instructions that do not depend on the missing load, but this only fills a short window (it runs out of useful work after roughly 10-20 cycles); dependent instructions must wait, so the processor eventually stalls.
Value prediction (Lipasti, Wilkerson and Shen, 1996) was proposed to keep executing past the miss, but it was fashionable in research and does not work in practice.
Runahead execution speculatively keeps executing past the miss, throws the results away, but starts prefetches for later cache misses; it wastes so much energy that it is not worth it.

Very large reorder buffers (e.g. Continual Flow Pipelines) let instructions dependent on the long-latency miss wait in the window while fetch continues, so independent work much later in the instruction stream can still be found.
Hardware prefetching guesses the next accessed lines (e.g. sequential cache lines in a loop) and compilers can insert prefetch instructions that load data into the cache ahead of use.
Switching to another OS task on a miss is not practical: it is expensive, requires a trap into the kernel, and the other task competes for the same cache.

questions.query: What is a retpoline and how does it work against Spectre?

key_points.text: A retpoline replaces an indirect jump or call with a call/ret sequence that pushes the real target and returns to it, so the CPU predicts the target with the return stack buffer instead of the poisonable indirect branch predictor (BTB).
The return predictor speculates to the address after the call, which is an infinite loop containing lfence/pause, so speculative execution is captured harmlessly until the real target is resolved.

Branch target injection (Spectre variant 2, CVE-2017-5715) trains the BTB from the attacker's own address space because the predictor does not record full source/destination addresses, causing a kernel indirect branch to speculatively execute an attacker-chosen gadget.
Speculatively executed instructions are discarded architecturally, but their effects on the cache remain and can be measured by cache-timing to leak secret data.

A retpoline does not prevent information disclosure directly; it only stops indirect branches from being used to steer speculation into a gadget, so other ways of speculatively executing a gadget are not covered.
Retpolines target Spectre variant 2 (branch target injection) and are generated by compiler options such as gcc -mindirect-branch=thunk-extern or LLVM -mretpoline.

questions.query: Replacing a 32-bit loop counter with 64-bit introduces crazy performance deviations with _mm_popcnt_u64 on Intel CPUs

key_points.text: On Sandy Bridge, Ivy Bridge and Haswell the popcnt instruction has a false dependency on its destination register: although it only writes it, it waits until the destination is ready (documented as Intel errata such as HSD146/SKL029).
The false dependency can carry across loop iterations, forming a dependency chain that prevents the processor from overlapping different iterations.
The unsigned vs uint64_t change does not cause the slowdown directly; it changes register allocation, which determines which false dependency chain forms.
Breaking the chain, e.g. zeroing the destination with xor before popcnt or using different registers, restores throughput; GCC from 4.9.2 compensates for this erratum while other compilers did not.
A likely reason is that popcnt runs on the same execution unit as bsf/bsr, which have a true output dependency (output unmodified for input 0); AMD processors do not show the false dependency.

questions.query: How do cache lines work? Which 64 bytes are brought into the cache when one byte is read?

key_points.text: Cache lines are aligned, non-overlapping blocks: a 64-byte line starts at an address divisible by 64, so the line holding a byte is found by clearing the low 6 address bits, which are the offset within the line.
A main memory access costs roughly 60-100 ns (hundreds of cycles) versus about 1-2 ns for L1, which is why the cache hierarchy exists.
Fetching a whole line exploits sequential access (reading index i makes i+1 likely) and DRAM burst mode, where each further sequential value costs little extra time.

Line granularity reduces address/tag overhead: the always-zero low bits need not be sent or stored, a per-line tag costs far less than per-word tags, and set associativity reduces stored address bits further.
The 64-byte line size is a trade-off between fetching bytes that are never used, the time to fetch and write back a line, and cache organization overhead.

questions.query: ARM Cortex-A8: what is the difference between VFP and NEON, and which should be used?

key_points.text: NEON is a SIMD unit that applies one instruction to multiple data elements (up to 16) in parallel; VFP is a conventional floating-point accelerator that performs one operation on one set of inputs.

VFP is fully IEEE-754 compliant and provides double precision, while ARMv7 NEON floating point is not fully IEEE-754 compliant, so compilers will not generate NEON floating-point code unless told full compliance is not required (e.g. -funsafe-math-optimizations or intrinsics).
On the Cortex-A8 the VFP is non-pipelined (a 'VFP Lite' unit), so NEON is faster for almost everything.
VFP's short-vector mode does not execute elements in parallel and is deprecated in ARMv7; software should use Advanced SIMD (NEON) for floating-point vector operations.
In ARMv8, NEON is fully IEEE-754 compliant and double precision is vectorized, so from a programmer's view there is little difference.
NEON can be used through arm_neon.h intrinsics, inline assembly, or by letting the compiler vectorize with -mfpu=neon.

questions.query: Is floating point math broken? Why is 0.1 + 0.2 not equal to 0.3?

key_points.text: Binary floating point (IEEE 754) represents numbers as an integer times a power of two, so rationals whose denominator is not a power of two, such as 0.1 = 1/10, cannot be represented exactly and are stored as approximations.
The constants 0.1, 0.2 and 0.3 are already approximations; the nearest doubles to 0.1 and 0.2 add up (after rounding) to a value different from the nearest double to 0.3, so the comparison fails.
Every positional base has the same limitation (e.g. 1/3 in decimal); binary simply cannot represent different fractions, such as tenths, exactly.
Do not compare floating-point values with ==; compare with a tolerance chosen for the application, keeping in mind that a fixed epsilon works only for values of a suitable magnitude.
IEEE 754 only requires each single operation's result to be within half a unit in the last place, so errors accumulate over repeated operations.

questions.query: What do clustered and non-clustered indexes actually mean?

key_points.text: There can be only one clustered index per table because the clustered index's leaf level is the table rows themselves (rows are kept in clustered-key order).
A non-clustered index is a separate structure whose entries point to the rows; a table can have many, but each extra index adds write cost.
Reading all columns via the clustered index is faster because no second lookup from index to table is needed; writes can be slower when data must be rearranged.
Clustering stores close key values physically near each other, which makes range scans (e.g. all orders for one CustomerID) fast.

Both index types are B-trees and the ordering is logical, not strictly physical: inserts cause page splits, pages are linked in key order but need not be contiguous, producing fragmentation that a rebuild reduces.
A non-clustered index's row locator is a physical RID on a heap, but the clustered index key when the table has a clustered index.

questions.query: What did MongoDB not being ACID compliant before v4 really mean?

key_points.text: MongoDB writes are atomic (ACID) at the level of a single document: an update to one document fully completes or not at all and readers never see it partially applied.
What was missing is multi-document / multi-collection transactions, e.g. you cannot atomically remove an item from inventory and add it to an order in another document.
Transaction-like behaviour across documents can be built on top of single-document atomicity with two-phase commit.

Workarounds: restructure the schema so related changes live in one document and use atomic modifiers, clean up out-of-sync records with a background process, or use a transactional RDBMS alongside MongoDB.
'Won't save correctly' also concerns durability: by default a write may be acknowledged before reaching disk, and write concern options control waiting for the journal or replicas.
From MongoDB 4.0, multi-document ACID transactions with snapshot isolation are supported.
Some applications can tolerate occasionally lost transactions or temporary inconsistency (Starbucks Does Not Use Two-Phase Commit); choose NoSQL when its behaviour meets requirements.

questions.query: Explanation of BASE (Basically Available, Soft state, Eventual consistency) terminology

key_points.text: BASE was coined by Eric Brewer, who formulated the CAP theorem: a distributed system cannot guarantee consistency, availability and partition tolerance at the same time.
A BASE system gives up consistency (in the CAP sense) in favour of availability.
Basically available means the system guarantees availability in the CAP sense.
Soft state means the system's state may change over time even without input, because of eventual consistency.
Eventual consistency means the system becomes consistent over time provided it receives no new input during that time.
Soft state implies stores need not be write-consistent or mutually consistent at all times.

questions.query: Database sharding vs partitioning

key_points.text: Partitioning is the generic term for dividing data across tables or databases; sharding is one specific type of it, namely horizontal partitioning.
Sharding replicates the schema across multiple instances/servers and divides the rows using a shard key that determines which instance holds the data.
Naive key schemes such as alphabetical ranges distribute data unevenly; a common technique is many logical shards mapped onto fewer physical shards (as Instagram did).
Horizontal partitioning splits rows while vertical partitioning splits columns (divides the schema); sharding refers only to the row-wise case.
Horizontal partitioning is usually within a single database instance, whereas sharding places partitions on different nodes so load and search can be spread across servers in parallel.
Partition pruning lets a query touch only the relevant partitions (e.g. a date range), which can improve performance by orders of magnitude.
Partitioning is done for manageability, performance or availability, e.g. very large tables or historical tables where only the newest partition is updated.

questions.query: What are OLTP and OLAP and what is the difference between them?

key_points.text: OLTP handles a large number of short online transactions (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE) on individual records, e.g. updating a user's email or a shopping cart.
OLTP emphasises fast query processing and data integrity in multi-access environments, measured in transactions per second, over detailed current data in a normalized (3NF) entity model.
OLAP handles a relatively low volume of complex aggregating queries over historical/archival data for analytics, and its effectiveness is measured by response time.
OLAP data is aggregated and stored in multidimensional schemas, usually a star schema.
Storage layout follows use: row-oriented storage makes per-record access cheap (OLTP), column-oriented storage makes whole-dataset aggregates cheap (OLAP).

questions.query: JOIN queries vs multiple queries: which is faster?

key_points.text: It depends on many factors, but with the right indexes and properly written joins one round trip is usually faster than several.
N+1 queries (one query per parent row) can drastically drop application performance; in benchmarks a JOIN is much faster.
For *-to-one relationships use a JOIN; for *-to-many relationships a second query (e.g. WHERE ... IN) can be faster because the join duplicates the parent data.
Chaining several LEFT JOINs over one-to-many relations multiplies rows (2,268,000 rows vs 165 across separate queries), using far more memory, so separate queries can win by orders of magnitude.
Connection latency matters: with a fast local connection separate queries cost little, while high per-query latency favours a single query.
Measure real-world numbers and compare against an acceptable threshold rather than against each other; if it performs well, choose the simpler solution.

questions.query: What is linting?

key_points.text: Linting is the process of running a program (a linter) that analyses source code for potential errors and problems.
lint was originally the name of a specific program that flagged suspicious and non-portable constructs (likely bugs) in C source code; the name became a generic term for such tools in any language.
A linter is a static checker: it examines the source code before it is compiled, linked and run, i.e. it is a static code analysis tool (like FindBugs for Java).

Linters check for stylistic as well as programmatic errors: formatting discrepancies, non-adherence to coding standards and conventions, and possible logical errors, which keeps code readable and maintainable.
Interpreted languages such as Python and JavaScript benefit especially from linting because they have no compile phase to surface errors before execution.

questions.query: What is the difference between pip and conda?

key_points.text: pip manages only Python packages and neglects non-Python library dependencies (HDF5, MKL, LLVM); conda is language-agnostic and installs packages containing software written in any language as well as Python packages.
conda can install the Python interpreter itself (and upgrade it), whereas pip needs an interpreter already installed by a system package manager or installer.
conda uses its own package format, so pip and conda are not interchangeable and do not interoperate, although pip can be used inside a conda environment for packages only available on PyPI.
conda is also an environment manager that creates isolated, language-agnostic environments natively, whereas pip relies on virtualenv for Python-only environments.

pip installs precompiled binary wheels when available (which are Python-version and OS specific, e.g. manylinux) or builds from source archives; conda installs only precompiled binary packages, removing the burden of compilation.

pip installs dependencies in a recursive serial loop without ensuring all are satisfied simultaneously, which can produce subtly broken environments; conda uses a SAT solver to verify that all requirements in the environment are met.

questions.query: Difference between Build Solution, Rebuild Solution, and Clean Solution in Visual Studio

key_points.text: Build performs an incremental build: it compiles and links only what has changed since the last build and skips projects it considers up to date.
Rebuild cleans and then builds from scratch, compiling everything regardless of whether the code changed.
Rebuild differs from Clean followed by Build: Rebuild cleans-then-builds each project one at a time, whereas Clean+Build first cleans all projects and then builds all.
Clean removes the build artifacts / intermediate files of the previous build (other files in bin and obj may remain).
Build is the normal and faster choice; Rebuild is needed when target components get out of sync or the incremental build failed to incorporate changes.

questions.query: Multi-language monorepo: pros and cons

key_points.text: Most tools assume one repository produces one deployable artifact, so adopting a monorepo means reworking that tooling or adopting tools designed for monorepos.

CI for code validation becomes much more complicated: conformance tests must support multiple languages, and checks must be selectively enabled so e.g. backend checks do not run on frontend-only changes; this is substantial release-engineering work.
A monorepo puts all eggs in one basket: a single leak or stolen laptop exposes all the code, while separate repositories reduce exposure.
Google makes monorepos work by dedicating many engineers to the tooling; organisations that succeed tend to be large, and smaller ones may not be able to follow that example.
At scale, how well an organisation does at code sharing and collaboration results from engineering culture and leadership, not from choosing a monorepo or polyrepo.

questions.query: What is the difference between step into and step over when debugging?

key_points.text: In gdb, step (step into) runs until the source line changes and so enters a called subroutine, while next (step over) does not trace into the subroutine but executes it and stops at the next line.
stepi and nexti are the analogous commands operating at the machine-instruction level instead of the source-line level.
Example: on a line that calls a function, step stops inside the called function, whereas next executes the call(s) and stops on the following line of the caller.

questions.query: How is Docker different from a virtual machine?

key_points.text: Containers (LXC/runC) run on and share the host OS kernel, while each VM runs its own full guest OS; so VMs give more isolation and guaranteed resources but are heavier, while containers are lightweight with weaker isolation.

A VM manager takes over CPU ring 0 / root mode and intercepts the guest OS's privileged calls to give it the illusion of owning the hardware; on x86 this was long thought impossible until VMware rewrote the guest's privileged instructions in memory.

Container isolation comes from kernel namespaces: global resources (network, disk, process view, memory) are wrapped so only processes in the same namespace can see them; because the kernel is shared, containers cannot run a different OS kernel and isolation is weaker (early container escapes existed).

Docker uses a layered union filesystem (AuFS): shared read-only base layers plus a per-container writable layer, and images store only diffs from their base, so many containers share one copy of the OS image on disk.
Containers start in seconds or less and need no pre-allocated memory for a separate OS copy, whereas VMs take minutes to boot, so thousands of containers can run on one host.

A Docker image snapshots the environment so the same image runs in dev, QA and prod, avoiding configuration drift and making the immutable-server pattern practical where large VM images made it laborious.

questions.query: What if kill -9 does not work?

key_points.text: SIGKILL always works if you have permission to signal the process, but it is not guaranteed to act immediately: signals are delivered asynchronously and queued while blocked.

A process blocked in a system call in uninterruptible sleep (state D in ps/top) cannot be killed until the call completes, because kernel code blocks signals to keep kernel invariants; a classic case is I/O to an unresponsive NFS server, and a hung syscall from a kernel/driver bug may leave reboot as the only remedy.
Even root cannot send a fatal signal to PID 1 (init); kernel threads are likewise immune to SIGKILL.

A zombie (state Z, <defunct>) has already exited and only holds a process-table entry because its parent has not read its exit status; it disappears when the parent reaps it or dies, so killing the parent (not the zombie) is the remedy.
Linux added the TASK_KILLABLE state (and since 2.6.25 SIGKILL interrupts NFS waits) so fatal signals can end some otherwise uninterruptible waits.
To diagnose a stuck process, inspect what it is doing with strace/dtrace, /proc/PID/syscall, kernel logs and lsof for the device or mount it is blocked on.

questions.query: When to use the different log levels (FATAL, ERROR, WARN, INFO, DEBUG, TRACE)

key_points.text: WARN is for things that may cause oddities but from which the application recovers automatically (failover to a backup server, retrying, missing secondary data, transient network loss); it might or might not be a problem.
ERROR is for failures fatal to an operation but not to the service/application, which need investigation or user/administrator intervention.
FATAL is reserved for errors forcing shutdown of the service/application to prevent (further) data loss; it should be very rare and is usually the last message of the process.
A practical heuristic: if the message should get a system administrator out of bed in the middle of the night it is an error (or fatal), otherwise a warning.
INFO records generally useful normal-operation events (service start/stop, configuration assumptions, significant transactions) and is the usual default level.
DEBUG/TRACE provide fine-grained context for diagnosing errors; levels must be used sparingly and noisy messages pruned, or logs lose signal and stop being used.

questions.query: What is the difference between SRE and DevOps?

key_points.text: DevOps is not just about code or systems; it is a very general term covering everything related to software delivery.
SRE, popularized by Google (Ben Treynor), is fundamentally what happens when you ask a software engineer to design an operations function.
SRE is heavily automated operations: the automation needed for mature infrastructure requires operations, engineering and development skills, with infrastructure managed as version-controlled code.
DevOps is a cultural way of thinking and working (sharing stories, developing empathy, organizational change), more than the sum of practices like infrastructure automation and continuous delivery.
The two are complementary: an effective SRE leverages DevOps practices.
SRE is a well-defined vertical role and you can have an SRE team, whereas DevOps is a horizontal role spanning teams along the delivery value chain, so a team of DevOps engineers is an oxymoron.
Which group owns what should not be implicit; it must be communicated explicitly.

questions.query: How to avoid retry storms in distributed services?

key_points.text: Too much traffic cannot be truly solved, only mitigated: without spending resources processing a request you cannot tell whether it is a retry, a duplicate of a succeeded request, or a DDoS.
For genuinely critical services, budget for heavily over-provisioned dedicated resources rather than relying on absorbing spikes.
On the client side, write sensible retry logic with an upper limit and graceful failure (return an error asking the user to try later) instead of endless retry loops.
On the server side the simplest tool is throttling: hard request limits, deciding deliberately which traffic to shed (e.g. distant requests) or how to spread the outage.
Intentionally returning a 503 at the gateway is far cheaper than letting the request through and timing out with a 504; return correct responses so clients adapt to current capacity.

questions.query: Infrastructure as code and TDD: is there a point in testing infrastructure described by states/roles?

key_points.text: Infrastructure tests fall into two categories: does it have everything the application needs to run, and does it not have anything superfluous.

The application's own test suite acts as a meta-test of the infrastructure, provided the infrastructure is built from scratch for each test run and the suite runs entirely on it without outside services.
From a security perspective, write tests against the infrastructure itself, e.g. port-scan a VM to catch unintended open ports introduced as a side effect of package installs.
Tests can check for unexpected file changes after the suite runs or unexpected processes in VMs/containers against whitelists, flagging undocumented changes from third-party package upgrades.
These second-category tests resemble classic operations hardening and intrusion checking.

questions.query: Optimistic vs pessimistic locking: when to use each

key_points.text: Optimistic locking reads a record together with a version number (or timestamp/checksum) and, on write-back, filters the update on that version so it applies atomically only if the record is unchanged; if the version changed the transaction is aborted and can be restarted.

Pessimistic locking locks the record for exclusive use until the transaction is finished; it gives better integrity than optimistic locking but the application must be designed carefully to avoid deadlocks.

Optimistic locking suits high-volume and three-tier systems where the client does not hold a database connection for the session (pooled connections cannot keep locks); pessimistic locking needs a direct connection or an external transaction ID, as in two-phase-commit distributed transactions (XA, COM+).

Pessimistic locking avoids conflicts by taking shared/exclusive locks that block conflicting writers, while optimistic locking lets the conflict happen and detects it at commit; both prevent the lost-update anomaly possible under Read Committed.

Pessimistic locking is preferable when contention is high (many concurrent updates, small frequently updated hotspot tables), because optimistic locking would waste effort rolling back conflicting transactions; optimistic locking fits when conflicts are rare.

For application-level (long, multi-request) transactions whose reads and writes run in separate database transactions, only optimistic locking via a version column catches lost updates; even Serializable isolation cannot.

questions.query: How does LMAX's disruptor pattern work?

key_points.text: The Disruptor is a way of sending messages between threads as efficiently as possible: an alternative to a queue built around a ring buffer, sharing features with SEDA and actors.
Publishing is two-phase: a producer first claims a slot in the ring buffer and fills the pre-existing entry, then commits it; the commit makes the entry visible to consumers.
Each consumer keeps track of its own consumed sequence, moving that responsibility off the ring buffer and reducing write contention.

Entries are pre-allocated and live forever, reducing garbage-collection cost and laying adjacent entries in adjacent memory so sequential reads exploit CPU caches; the design avoids locks, CAS and even memory barriers where possible (e.g. a single writer).

The ring is bounded: when full, writers wait for the slowest reader; readers can declare dependencies forming an acyclic graph so a dependent reader never passes the reader it depends on, and annotating readers write to different fields/cache lines.

Compared with actors, the Disruptor uses one thread per consumer rather than an N:M model, and its end-of-batch callback lets slow consumers batch work without timeout-based batching that hurts latency.

Producers obtain monotonically increasing sequence numbers; the slot is sequence & (bufferSize-1) because the size is a power of two, and a producer waits if its sequence would exceed the slowest consumer's by more than the buffer size.

questions.query: Using Kafka as a CQRS event store: good idea?

key_points.text: It depends on the kind of event sourcing: Kafka fits downstream event processing where real-world facts are recorded, but not an application-controlled source of truth where business logic emits events.

Event sourcing needs to load the event stream of a single entity; Kafka cannot do this efficiently: topic-per-entity is impractical (each partition is a directory, ZooKeeper znode pressure) and topic-per-type forces reading every entity's events.
Kafka lacks optimistic concurrency (a conditional write only if the entity's last event is #x), so conflicting events cannot be prevented without a stateful serialized writer per shard.

According to one of Kafka's original authors, Kafka works well as the log for event sourcing: it is fault-tolerant, scales to large data sizes and has a built-in partitioning model (used this way at LinkedIn, with Samza support).

Kafka retains published messages for a configurable retention period and the expectation is that they are eventually deleted, though Kafka's own documentation calls its large stored logs an excellent backend for event sourcing.

Event sourcing persists state-changing events per entity stream; current state is a left fold of the entity's events, and a good event store must append and load by entity id, delete an entity's events, and offer real-time subscriptions to feed CQRS read models.
Kafka's at-least-once delivery can leave duplicates in the store, and Kafka offers no place to persist aggregate snapshots, so replay gets slower over time.

questions.query: Why isn't an RDBMS partition tolerant in the CAP theorem, and why is it available?

key_points.text: In CAP, consistency means a query gets the same answer whichever node handles it; availability means every request gets an answer (not high throughput); partition tolerance means the system keeps functioning despite a partition rather than fixing it.

Under default configurations RDBMSs such as MySQL count as CA because they shut down or disconnect nodes when a partition occurs, avoiding the partition instead of operating through it, whereas Cassandra and MongoDB keep partitioned nodes serving.

A CP system keeps answering only from nodes still connected to the master that handles writes, so the other side is unavailable; an AP system lets replicas answer regardless (or elect a new master, or is masterless), so both sides reply with possibly different state.

CAP classification depends on configuration: MySQL master-slave replication is CA by default, sacrificing partition tolerance because partitioned slaves may elect a second master; MySQL's clustered configuration prioritises CP and shuts down without enough live nodes.

CAP availability has little to do with a master/slave setup: Cassandra is masterless and highly available, and in master/slave there is no reason to stop answering reads when the master dies, though writes may be suspended.
As a rule of thumb, the master-slave model is generally used for CA systems and the hash ring for AP systems.

questions.query: Conflict-free replicated data types (CRDT) vs Paxos or Raft: when to use which

key_points.text: Paxos enforces a total order on updates so every replica agrees on how the state evolves, whereas CRDTs assume concurrent updates and guarantee that replicas which have seen the same updates, in any order, converge to the same state.

Paxos-replicated data is simple to reason about (equivalent to an unreplicated object) but cannot be updated during a network partition and has higher latency because replicas must synchronise before replying.

CRDTs give weaker guarantees: replicas temporarily diverge and can expose states impossible in a sequential object, making them harder to reason about, but they remain updatable under partition and reply with low latency, syncing in the background.
Use a CRDT if you can: it gives much better performance and enables working offline and merging later; but not every problem can be designed as a CRDT, and then Paxos solves the hard problems.

Even when using Paxos, limit the work done through it: reserve it for operations such as master election and let a replicated master (delegating shards) handle most decisions so it does not become a bottleneck.
Implementing Paxos in practice is much harder than claiming it; Google's Chubby paper describes the difficulties a real-world Paxos implementation meets.

questions.query: Compiling an application for use in highly radioactive environments: how to detect and correct soft errors from single event upsets in embedded software

key_points.text: Use redundancy with voting: run the same computation or hardware three or more times (triple modular redundancy) and take a majority vote to mask a corrupted result, resetting or failing safe when results disagree.
Implement watchdog timers and periodic sanity-check routines so that a lock-up or loss of progress is detected and the system is reset.
Protect memory with error-correcting codes or checksums (CRC) in software, or preferably use hardware with built-in ECC; software ECC costs processing time, which is a trade-off.
Keep as much code and constant data as possible in ROM/NVM and refresh registers and variables from NVM at run time rather than trusting initialised RAM (.data/.bss) contents.
Resilient algorithms and data structures (the faulty-RAM model of Finocchi and Italiano) guarantee correct output up to a bound on the number of memory faults.
Replicate whole nodes and use a quorum protocol (e.g. Raft) over checksummed state-machine state so only majority-agreed state changes are applied and self-detected faulty nodes reboot.
Choose safety-oriented MCUs with lock-step cores, built-in ECC and windowed watchdogs, and apply defensive programming with a coding standard such as MISRA.

questions.query: What makes a kernel/OS real-time? Is a real-time scheduler enough?

key_points.text: The defining property of a real-time OS is the ability to guarantee a maximum latency between an external interrupt and the start of its handler; the bound need not be particularly short.
A real-time scheduler offers completely predictable thread scheduling, typically with many priority levels and priority inheritance to avoid priority inversion.
A real-time scheduler alone does not make an RTOS: it is necessary, but predictable behaviour is also needed in other parts of the OS.

General-purpose OSes aim for fair resource allocation and good overall performance (time-slicing, dynamic priority adjustment), which is at odds with worst-case latency guarantees; an RTOS leaves developer-set priorities alone even if low-priority tasks starve.
Simpler hardware is more predictable (ISA more than PCI more than PCI-E), but many real-time requirements can be met on commodity hardware.

questions.query: What is the power implication of encrypting battery-powered sensor traffic?

key_points.text: For a battery-powered sensor, most of the energy goes to RF transmission, not to CPU cycles spent on encryption.
Every additional transmitted bit costs more power than the encryption computation, so message expansion matters more than cipher cost.
A naive block mode such as AES-CBC can increase the message size to whole blocks, adding transmitted bits.
AES in counter (CTR) mode generates stream-cipher bits so ciphertext need not grow, and suits unreliable links where packets may be lost.
CTR mode requires keeping counters synchronised (periodically sending the counter adds overhead) and never reusing a counter, because keystream reuse leads directly to data recovery.

questions.query: What makes smartphones tilt-sensitive, and do the sensors still work in zero gravity?

key_points.text: Tilt sensing uses MEMS accelerometers (and gyroscopes): moving micro-structures fabricated on a chip with integrated-circuit processes such as etching and deposition.
The sensors detect displacement of a tiny suspended mass (interleaved comb teeth / spring-mass) through changes in capacitance.
An accelerometer feels gravity as a constant 1 g acceleration and uses that vector to find which way is down, giving tilt.
In zero gravity or free fall the chips still sense acceleration, but they lose the gravity reference vector, so the phone cannot tell up from down.
MEMS gyroscopes replace the spinning disk with a structure vibrating at high frequency to sense rotation.
Phones typically combine a three-axis accelerometer with gyroscopes and a magnetometer, sometimes in one small IMU package that does the maths internally.

questions.query: When is CRC more appropriate to use than MD5/SHA1 for error detection on embedded hardware?

key_points.text: CRC is designed to detect random, unintentional errors such as line noise, interference or distortion.
CRC is computationally much less complex than MD5/SHA1 and much easier to implement in embedded hardware, even as packaged ICs.
CRC gives no protection against malicious modification: it is a linear, easily reversible function, so it is unsuitable for security checks or signatures.
For security use cryptographic hashes, but MD5 and SHA-1 have known collisions and are deprecated; SHA-2 or SHA-3 should be used.
When CRC is sufficient, use a good standard polynomial.

questions.query: Why don't all companies buy developers the best hardware?

key_points.text: Many managers expect highly paid developers to be just as productive with poor tools and working conditions; if the company can afford it, not giving developers what they need to be productive is irrational (what 'good tools' means depends on the job).
Mediocre hardware causes slow builds, which makes developers reluctant to build, lowering productivity and causing quality problems and broken builds.

The hardware cost is visible and quantifiable, while the productivity lost by not upgrading is invisible to those above the tech department and rests on unprovable assumptions, so the purchase needs heavy justification.

Price versus benefit is a sliding scale: top-end machines cost much more, depreciate faster and give negligible gains over near-top machines for general business development; cashflow limits spending, so mid-range machines are the sensible choice.
Standardised hardware and software images reduce IT support cost; a constant churn of new top-end machines needs extra IT staff and swap-over downtime.
Working conditions such as tiny desks in a crowded bullpen with no partitions also damage developer productivity, independent of the machines.

questions.query: How to distribute development and bug fix tasks in a scrum team with a constant stream of bugs

key_points.text: A constant stream of bug reports signals a product quality problem; the first priority is getting the product into shape through root-cause analysis of bugs, refactoring and a solid unit-test suite.
A single engineer absorbing all development and bug work is not a sustainable team setup.

Most bugs are not emergencies: they should be reported and categorised by someone else, and the developer should only be interrupted for emergency bugs, finishing the current task first with an undistracted mind.
Keep development tasks small (about a day) and schedule incoming bugs for the next day, accepting that some sprint items will not be done.
With fluctuating incoming bugs Kanban fits more naturally; alternatively represent bug fixing as a ticket in the sprint or reduce the sprint size.
Rushed feature work creates bugs that force more rushing; break the cycle with fewer, better-tested releases and stop new features until a release is stable.

questions.query: Explaining to laypeople why bootstrapping works

key_points.text: Since we cannot resample the population, we can either assume a model for it and simulate samples, or use the sample itself as a stand-in for the population and resample from it to see how variable the statistic is.
Resampling does not estimate the population distribution; the sample is taken as a model of the population, and resampling estimates the sampling distribution of the statistic.

Formally, the statistic is a functional T of the distribution function; the bootstrap applies T to the empirical distribution F_n in place of F, which works when F_n is close to F and T is smooth enough.

The bootstrap principle: sampling with replacement behaves on the original sample the way the original sample behaves on the population; there are examples where the principle fails and the bootstrap is not the answer to every problem.
Accessible treatments include Efron and Tibshirani's 1986 Statistical Science article (judged good) and Efron and Diaconis's 1983 Scientific American article (judged a failed attempt).
Each bootstrap resample is drawn with replacement to the original sample size, and the variation across the resample estimates shows how accurate the original estimate is.

questions.query: Who has the final say in product decisions between product owners, UX and developers

key_points.text: Team decision processes fail both ways: teams immobilised by consensus at large companies and ego-driven founder decisions at startups; agile/lean frameworks do not address this directly.
Collaboration is not consensus: a team needs a single leader with shot-calling authority who also bears ultimate responsibility, calling the shots when consensus is too slow or costly.

The answerer favours the product manager as ultimate decision authority within the product team, for commercial alignment, with escalation up to the CEO, though other roles may lead depending on the situation.
Establish clear specialist roles: developers decide code issues and UX professionals decide usability issues, so decision making incorporates specialisation.

questions.query: What mistakes should an indie game developer never make?

key_points.text: A major pitfall is spending too much effort on the framework, tools or engine instead of the game itself; start by working out how to make the game entertaining, not by coding a math library.
Choosing too big a project (such as an MMORPG) and poor planning lead to burnout; games take a long time, so set small, realistic goals.
Set a fixed release date and stick to it, do not keep the game secret, and engage the community and early alpha testers and review sites.
Do not ignore marketing: an unknown indie must start building a brand and talking to the community as early as possible.
Do not underestimate decent content tools: they need not be high-tech but must be stable and usable, especially for content-heavy games or teams.
Avoid over-attention to polish early: if the concept is not fun with placeholder boxes, art time will not make it fun.
Going full-time requires a business plan: revenue streams, burn rate, cash reserves and how long development can run before shipping.

questions.query: When should I use a fixed or variable time step in a game loop?

key_points.text: Physics update rate should not be tied to the display frame rate; step physics with constant deltas using a time accumulator, taking as many fixed steps per rendered frame as needed.

A variable time step produces variable results that are hard to debug: integrators simulate at discrete points in time, and with stiff spring constraints tiny changes in dt can make the simulation explode.

Delta-time (variable) updates are often implemented badly and lead to inconsistent collision detection and physics; doing it right needs e.g. a Verlet integrator instead of Euler and ray-based collision detection.

With a fixed step, the game logic is updated multiple times per rendered frame to catch up with real time and then drawn once; interpolating graphics between states is only for visual smoothness, not game logic.
If updates are expensive and fall behind, catching up requires more and more update steps per frame, so the timestep can spin out of control.

An alternative is to run physics at a fixed timestep on a separate thread and have the game interpolate or extrapolate from the two most recent physics states; interpolation adds lag, extrapolation adds uncertainty.

questions.query: How can I determine whether a 2D point is within a polygon?

key_points.text: Ray casting (crossing number): cast a ray from the point and count how many polygon edges it crosses; an odd count means inside, even means outside (Jordan curve theorem). It works for convex, concave and holed polygons.
