Run a cheap axis-aligned bounding-box test first: a point outside the polygon's min/max x and y cannot be inside, which avoids the expensive test.
The bounding-box pre-check can slow things down when most query points lie inside the box, because the crossing test is nearly as fast; precompute bounding boxes for polygons that rarely change.

The winding-number / angle-summation alternative sums the oriented angles from the point to consecutive vertices: 360 degrees means inside, 0 means outside; it is more robust near edges but much slower.
Ray casting can misclassify points very close to an edge or when the ray hits a vertex, because of limited floating-point precision and degenerate crossings.

In Eric Haines' benchmarks the crossings test performs well, angle summation is by far the slowest, and grid-based subdivision of the polygon into in/out cells makes tests very fast even for polygons with over 1000 edges.

questions.query: Why does Monte Carlo tree search work when a real opponent's behavior is not random?

key_points.text: Plain (pure) Monte Carlo search, which only averages the results of many random playouts, must be distinguished from Monte Carlo Tree Search; for plain Monte Carlo the concern about treating opponent moves as equally likely is correct.
MCTS gradually builds a search tree (Expansion step) and traverses that tree with a much more sophisticated, non-random strategy (Selection step).

Once a node's children are in the tree, Selection steers most further iterations toward the opponent's best reply (the instant loss for us), so the node's value no longer reflects uniformly random opponent moves.
In the limit of infinite search time, the bias of Selection makes the average evaluation converge to the correct minimax evaluation.
Random playouts are still informative because from a very strong position a player is more likely to win even when both sides play randomly.

questions.query: How do raymarch shaders work?

key_points.text: Ray tracing needs an exact ray-primitive intersection function and tests the ray against all relevant primitives to pick the closest hit.
Ray marching uses a distance function that, for a point on the ray, estimates how close it is to the surface instead of an exact intersection, and steps ('marches') along the ray.

Each step moves forward by the (conservative) distance estimate so the ray never tunnels through the surface, repeating until the point is within a threshold of the surface or a maximum step count is reached.
The resulting surface depth is used to infer normals and ambient occlusion from nearby samples and then to light and colour the pixel.
Ray tracing's non-local data traversal and varied intersection workloads historically kept it on CPUs; only recent specialised GPU hardware and APIs made it tractable on GPUs.

questions.query: How to generate huge pseudo-infinite procedurally generated wilderness worlds with Perlin noise?

key_points.text: Noise is not random: it is random-looking but given by a repeatable mathematical formula, so all of the world's information is encoded in the formula.

Evaluate the formula at the world coordinates of whatever area is needed; because the function is continuous, adjacent regions generated at different times join seamlessly, allowing a potentially infinite world.
If the world never changes nothing needs to be stored, since any point can be recomputed; a deformable world like Minecraft must save each chunk once it is created or modified.
There is no need to generate the whole world at once; regions can be built asynchronously as the player visits them.
In Perlin noise the first octave sets the general shape of the terrain and later octaves add finer detail, so the first octave's wavelength controls how large landmasses are.
To keep a landmass in the centre, subtract an increasing amount from the heightmap with distance from the centre and then normalise the noise.

questions.query: Why do ChatGPT jailbreaks work and why are they hard to prevent?

key_points.text: The setup that makes an LLM a well-behaved chatbot is largely a hidden system/pre-prompt that the model processes the same way as user input; it sets context but is not privileged.
The LLM is a text-prediction engine; given conflicting instructions it has no easy way to prioritise and may base predictions on newer instructions instead of older ones.
Many jailbreaks obey the letter of the rules but reframe the conversation, e.g. having the chatbot write fiction from an imagined perspective other than its assigned identity.
It is very hard to detect and block jailbreaks without also blocking intended uses, because conversations can become subjective, allegorical or multi-layered.
LLMs are internally complex and driven by vast data, so developers cannot exert detailed control over them and do not fully understand how they perform.

questions.query: How do I count tokens before sending an OpenAI API request?

key_points.text: Tokens can be counted programmatically with tiktoken, a fast BPE tokenizer used for OpenAI models (or interactively with OpenAI's Tokenizer tool).
Given a string and an encoding (e.g. cl100k_base), a tokenizer splits the text into a list of tokens; GPT models see text in the form of tokens.
Knowing the token count tells you whether the text is too long for the model to process and how much an API call costs, since usage is priced by token.
Different models use different encodings: cl100k_base for gpt-4/gpt-3.5-turbo/text-embedding-ada-002, p50k_base for text-davinci models, r50k_base for GPT-3.
Chat models' message-based formatting makes token counting harder; if a conversation exceeds the model's maximum you must truncate, omit or shrink text, and removed messages are lost to the model.
Very long conversations near the limit get incomplete replies, e.g. a 4090-token gpt-3.5-turbo conversation has its reply cut off after 6 tokens.

questions.query: Should I normalize word2vec's word vectors before using them?

key_points.text: If downstream applications only care about direction (e.g. cosine similarity), normalize and forget about length.
Normalizing vectors to unit length before similarity calculation makes cosine similarity and dot product equivalent (Levy et al., 2015).
For similarity and word-relation tasks, using normalised word vectors was found to improve performance, so vector length is typically ignored (Wilson and Schakel, 2015).
Normalizing loses the notion of length that vectors had after training, which is not a good idea if the application needs aspects like word significance.

Vector length carries information: a word used consistently in similar contexts gets a longer vector than a same-frequency word used in varied contexts; length plus term frequency measures word significance (Schakel and Wilson, 2015).

questions.query: What is the temperature parameter in GPT models and how does it introduce randomness?

key_points.text: The next token is predicted from a distribution softmax(x_i/T) over the vocabulary, where T is the temperature.
Randomness is introduced when choosing the next token: the temperature-scaled distribution is sampled from (the example code reweights log-probabilities by temperature and draws from a multinomial).
Low temperature makes the model greedy: other tokens get small probability, output is likely correct but boring with little variation.
High temperature lets the model choose lower-probability words, giving more diverse text but more grammar mistakes and nonsense.
Chollet's Deep Learning with Python (chapter 12) gives a sampling example for temperature.

questions.query: Is the Chinese room an explanation of how ChatGPT works?

key_points.text: Searle's Chinese Room shows it is hard to locate intelligence in a system from its inputs and outputs; ChatGPT manipulates symbols by opaque rules without grounding for what they mean.
LLMs are trained only on more written language, never experience; like learning words from a dictionary defined by other unknown words, this relates to the symbol grounding problem.

One can argue the system-level intelligence is still real and resides in the rules (focusing on whole-system behaviour), side-stepping hard problems like subjective experience; the argument has critics.
The Chinese room is a thought experiment meant as a reductio against the computational theory of mind / strong AI, not a functional description of a real machine; LLMs are not realizations of it.
We cannot be sure humans are not very sophisticated Chinese rooms: AI matching human performance with the same architectures would create an apparent paradox.

questions.query: In a Transformer, why sum positional encoding to the embedding rather than concatenate it?

key_points.text: Concatenation requires fixing a priori the dimensionalities d_t for token and d_p for position (d = d_t + d_p), reducing the size devoted to tokens.
Adding is potentially a superset of concatenation: training could converge to token and position vectors occupying complementary subsets of dimensions with the rest zero.
Summing leaves the use of the d dimensions to the optimization process instead of assuming an optimal partition and adding a new hyperparameter to tune.
With addition the representation is not restricted by a hard split of vector components and uses the whole representation space.

questions.query: How to select the number of hidden layers and memory cells in an LSTM?

key_points.text: There is usually no rule for the number of hidden nodes; it must be figured out per case by trial and error.
A rule of thumb to prevent over-fitting is to keep hidden neurons below N_h = N_s / (alpha * (N_i + N_o)), with alpha an arbitrary scaling factor usually 2-10.
You want to limit the number of free parameters (nonzero weights) to a small portion of the degrees of freedom in the data, N_s * (N_i + N_o).
Dropout layers bring the effective branching factor of the network well below its actual mean branching factor.

questions.query: How do I teach a large language model new knowledge?

key_points.text: Document retrieval: store pre-computed embeddings of many documents in a vector database, look up relevant documents by embedding similarity at query time and append a text chunk to the prompt.
Retrieval needs no model training and works even with black-box models such as GPT-4; the model draws on the provided text more accurately than on what it saw in training.
Parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods, in particular LoRA, allow tweaking a model on far more reasonable hardware than full training (even high-end consumer hardware for LLaMA).
Fine-tuning tunes the model on all of your data rather than a single retrieved chunk, and can even teach a new language or turn a foundation model into a chat model.

questions.query: Understanding Kafka topics and partitions: how producers pick partitions, how consumer groups map to partitions, and who tracks offsets

key_points.text: The producer decides the target partition: the explicit partition id if given, otherwise hash of the message key modulo the number of partitions, otherwise round robin when there is no key.
Within one consumer group each partition is processed by only one consumer; with fewer consumers than partitions a consumer gets several partitions, and consumers beyond the partition count sit idle.

Offset state is managed by the group coordinator (an elected broker) which records commits in the internal __consumer_offsets topic; consumers heartbeat to it, and commits can be made manual by disabling enable.auto.commit and calling commitSync/commitAsync.
When messages have expired under topic-level retention, a consumer with no valid offset starts according to auto.offset.reset (earliest or latest).

A partition is an ordered, immutable, append-only commit log whose messages carry sequential ids (offsets); partitions are the unit of parallelism, let a topic scale beyond one broker, and are replicated across brokers for fault tolerance.

questions.query: Orchestrating microservices: orchestration vs choreography for business processes that span several services

key_points.text: There are two styles for processes that span service boundaries: orchestration relies on a central brain that drives the process like a conductor, while choreography tells each part its job and lets it react to others like dancers.

The downside of orchestration is that the central service becomes too much of a governing authority, producing a few smart 'god' services directing anemic CRUD services; heavily orchestrated systems tend to be brittle with a higher cost of change.

In choreography services emit events asynchronously and others subscribe and react, which is more decoupled, but the business process is only implicit, so extra monitoring is needed to track processes across service boundaries.

Orchestration is commonly implemented with business process / workflow tooling: BPM engines such as Camunda, earlier WS-BPEL platforms in SOA, and modern engines like Netflix Conductor or Zeebe, or lighter frameworks such as Camel or Spring Integration.
Orchestration is a compound pattern; the orchestrator often relies on compensating transactions and a state repository (dehydration) to manage long-running compositions.

The API Gateway pattern puts a front-end server between clients and microservices that offers client-tailored coarse-grained APIs, fans requests out to several services and aggregates results, and encapsulates the services so they can evolve without affecting clients.

questions.query: 2PC vs sagas for distributed transactions: when and why use one over the other

key_points.text: Two-phase commit suits immediate (short) transactions, while sagas suit long-running transactions.
With 2PC, provided every participating system and network follows the protocol, the whole transaction across systems is committed or rolled back as a unit.
A saga splits a transaction into multiple steps that can span long periods, e.g. booking an itinerary of connecting flights run by different airlines.
2PC favours consistency while a saga degrades to eventual consistency; when consistency matters more than availability (CAP) a system transaction protocol like 2PC may be needed.
A saga is a technology-agnostic domain-modelling concept, whereas 2PC is a technology-specific protocol that requires platforms implementing it, which ties the design to those vendors.
The choice maps to the distinction between system transactions and business transactions (as in Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture).

questions.query: What are the underlying data structures used for Redis?

key_points.text: Redis internally uses simple dynamic strings, dictionaries (hash tables), doubly linked lists, skip lists, ziplists and intsets (zipmaps deprecated), and OBJECT ENCODING shows which encoding a key uses.

Small lists, hashes and sorted sets are stored as ziplists: entries stored inline without pointers, which saves memory but costs CPU (O(n) lookup, reallocation on insert), so Redis uses them only below configurable size thresholds.

Small sets of integers are stored as intsets: sorted integer arrays searched by binary search, in 16/32/64-bit variants, converted to a hash table when they grow past a threshold (default 512) or a non-integer is added.
Sorted sets use a skip list together with a dictionary that maps each element to its score, so ZSCORE is O(1); the skip list allows duplicate scores and has a back pointer for reverse traversal.
Dictionaries are hash tables with incremental rehashing: two tables are kept and one bucket is migrated on each access, avoiding an expensive one-shot resize.
Redis strings are Simple Dynamic Strings that store the length as a prefix, making strlen O(1) and strings binary safe.

questions.query: Scaling solutions for MySQL: replication vs clustering vs sharding

key_points.text: MySQL replication uses a master that takes writes and one or more slaves that serve reads; it is used for splitting read load, hot backups and failover, and needs load balancing across nodes.
MySQL replication is asynchronous, so replication lag means not every node has the freshest data and the application must be replication-aware when it needs current data.

MySQL NDB Cluster is a distributed in-memory shared-nothing engine with synchronous replication and automatic partitioning; multi-table queries must fetch from several nodes so network latency slows them, and the whole database must fit in memory.
Sharding splits data into shards on different servers to scale horizontally, but the application must know where each piece of data lives.
Cluster's main selling point is high availability with no single point of failure, whereas with replication a master failure requires switching to a replica with some downtime.
For most web applications the recommended approach is replication with a load balancer, plus sharding of the specific huge tables.

questions.query: What are the main differences between Apache Flink and Apache Storm?

key_points.text: Storm guarantees at-least-once processing using record-level acknowledgments, while Flink provides exactly-once using a variant of the Chandy-Lamport algorithm: sources inject markers, operators checkpoint state on receiving them, and on failure all operators reset to the last committed marker; this is lighter than per-record acks.
Flink's DataStream API offers high-level functions such as Map, GroupBy, Window and Join, whereas in Storm much of this must be implemented by hand in bolts.
Both Storm and Flink aim for low latency through pipelined data transfers between tasks; Flink also supports batch processing natively while Storm has no batch capability.
Storm's Trident offers an exactly-once high-level API but is based on mini-batches, making it closer to Spark than to Flink.

Flink's adjustable latency comes from buffering records for network transfer and sending a buffer when it is full or a timeout expires; the timeout bounds buffering delay but gives no hard end-to-end latency guarantee.
Flink also handles backpressure through its network buffer pools, lets operators keep user-defined state that is checkpointed with exactly-once guarantees, and has a rich windowing system.

questions.query: How do Prometheus rate() and increase() work and differ?

key_points.text: increase(counter[d]) is exactly rate(counter[d]) multiplied by the range in seconds (e.g. increase over 5s = rate over 5s * 5).
Prometheus uses only the raw samples inside the range window and needs at least two of them; with a range equal to the scrape interval, rate and increase return nothing.
The rate is computed from the first and last samples in the window, which span less than the window, and the increase is extrapolated to cover the full range.
Because of extrapolation and uneven sample spacing, rate and increase can return fractional values for integer counters.
The first increment of a newly appearing counter is not counted, since Prometheus cannot know when the counter was zero.

Increase between the last sample before the window and the first sample in it is missed, so increase over 1h does not equal the sum of 1m increases; counter resets inside the window also complicate the calculation.

questions.query: What is a CRDT in distributed systems?

key_points.text: A CRDT is a data structure for achieving strong eventual consistency and monotonicity: replicas are updated without remote synchronization, may diverge, and can always be merged safely so that conflicts are mathematically impossible.
The CRDT merge is idempotent, commutative and associative, so repeated and out-of-order updates are safe.

There are two styles: state-based (convergent) CRDTs that ship whole state, using more bandwidth, and operation-based (commutative) CRDTs that ship updates and need extra delivery guarantees from the middleware; each can emulate the other.
A CRDT's possible values form a join semilattice, a partially ordered set with a least upper bound, and state only grows monotonically so replicas converge on the LUB.
Under CAP, CRDTs give the strongest consistency available to available/partition-tolerant (AP) systems, which are eventually consistent.
Real uses include Riak's CRDTs (League of Legends chat, Bet365) and SoundCloud's Roshi, a last-writer-wins timestamped set that discards stale updates and converges via read repair.

questions.query: Why does tan(pi/2) return 16331239353195370.0 instead of infinity?

key_points.text: pi (and pi/2) is not exactly representable as a binary double, so the closest representable approximation is used as the input.
The binary approximation of pi/2 is slightly less than the true pi/2, so tan returns a very large finite value rather than infinity.
The computed tan() is correct for the actual (rounded) input; the discrepancy comes from the input representation, not from tan.
For the same reason math.sin(math.pi) returns about 1.22e-16 rather than 0.
Every finite binary float is exactly representable as a finite decimal (the reverse is not true, e.g. 0.1), so Decimal(float), as_integer_ratio() or hex() reveal the exact value stored.
Because almost all machines now use IEEE 754 double precision, math.pi has the same value across almost all platforms.

questions.query: Why do we still do symbolic math if most practical problems only have numerical solutions?

key_points.text: Numerical methods can fail (e.g. Newton's method on x^(1/3) = 0), and understanding the underlying mathematics is needed to detect when a method is not working and to fix it.
Some problems are easier to solve symbolically than with a numerical method.

The stability, efficiency and accuracy of numerical algorithms cannot be established numerically; designing and analysing numerical methods (and knowing whether an approximation is good enough) requires symbolic mathematics.
Equations such as x^2 = 2 have no rational solution; producing rationals arbitrarily close to the solution just reinvents the real numbers in a more cumbersome form.
Symbolic formulas carry structure and meaning and give insight, whereas numerical results are unstructured values.
Many branches of mathematics (e.g. group theory, topology) concern objects more general than numbers and cannot be done numerically.

questions.query: What is the difference between full text search and LIKE in SQL

key_points.text: LIKE gives 100% precision with no concession for recall, whereas full-text search lets you tune down precision to gain recall.
Full-text search implementations use an inverted index whose keys are individual terms and whose values are the sets of records (documents) containing each term.
Full-text search is optimized to compute intersections and unions of these record sets and usually provides a ranking algorithm scoring how strongly a record matches the query.
LIKE must scan linearly: on an unindexed column it is a full scan, and a pattern with a leading wildcard forces examining every index key.
Information retrieval systems can support leading wildcards efficiently by pre-compiling auxiliary structures (e.g. suffix trees) over the terms.
Full-text search adds lexical analysis/tokenization and morphological analysis/stemming that collapses word variants into one index term.

questions.query: Is cosine similarity identical to l2-normalized euclidean distance

key_points.text: For l2-normalized vectors, expanding (x-y)^T(x-y) gives ||x-y||^2 = 2 - 2 x^T y = 2 - 2 cos(angle(x,y)).
Hence the squared Euclidean distance between unit vectors is proportional to the cosine distance.

Even with normalized data and a scale-invariant algorithm, results can still differ from cosine because the relationship involves squaring (Euclidean distance itself is not linear in cosine distance).

questions.query: What is the difference between lemmatization and stemming

key_points.text: Both stemming and lemmatization reduce inflectional (and sometimes derivationally related) forms of a word to a common base form, reducing morphological variation.

Stemming is a crude heuristic/rule-based process that chops off word endings, often including derivational affixes; lemmatization uses a vocabulary and morphological analysis to remove inflectional endings and return the dictionary form (lemma).

A stemmer operates on a single word without context, so it cannot distinguish meanings that depend on part of speech; lemmatization can use POS/context to pick the right lemma (e.g. 'meeting' noun vs verb).
A stem need not be a valid word as long as related words map to it, whereas a lemma is a linguistically valid dictionary word.
Some relations, such as 'better' to 'good', are missed by stemming because they require a dictionary lookup.

Stemmers are simpler and faster; lemmatization is more expensive (needs lexica, POS tagging), so stemming suffices for large-scale IR with short queries while lemmatization suits accuracy-critical tasks.

questions.query: How to find nearest neighbors in high-dimensional data efficiently

key_points.text: In high dimensions the curse of dimensionality makes traditional structures such as the k-d tree about as slow as brute-force search.
The remedy is approximate nearest neighbor search, trading some accuracy for speed: e.g. LSH, forests of randomized k-d trees (FLANN), and (locally optimized) product quantization.
Dimensionality reduction such as PCA or ICA can show whether all dimensions are needed and allow searching in fewer dimensions with similar quality.

The number of dimensions does not determine the distance metric; the choice depends on the data distribution, feature covariance and coordinate space, and Euclidean (or Mahalanobis) is usually a sound default.
Features must be rescaled (e.g. subtract mean, divide by standard deviation) or large-scale features dominate the distance.
Partitioning the data into Voronoi cells around sampled centers lets a query first find the nearest center and then search only that cell, far fewer distance computations than brute force.

questions.query: How do you do load testing and capacity planning for web sites?

key_points.text: No one can give a generic capacity answer; you must benchmark your own specific workload by trying it and seeing where the system buckles.
The method is an iterative loop: put a test scenario in place, add monitoring, add traffic, evaluate results, remediate, and repeat until satisfied.
The test environment should approximate production hardware as closely as possible; otherwise results must be extrapolated or scaled.
Monitor how many requests per second get through before user response time exceeds a target (e.g. two seconds), together with RAM, CPU and disk usage of the components under test.
Capacity planning starts with measuring response time versus load, which is not linear; choose a response-time target and find the resources needed to meet it at a given load.
Performance should be measured in time units because that is what users care about; %CPU and IOPS are system-specific surrogates usable only once the system has been measured in pre-production.

questions.query: Can invariant (property-based) testing with QuickCheck replace unit testing?

key_points.text: No: example-based unit tests remain necessary as regression tests, attached to a bug report and kept in the codebase so the bug never comes back.
In principle any unit test can be replaced by a test with randomly generated inputs, even for imperative code where the input is the sequence of statements/calls.
Whether it is worth building the random data generator, and whether it can be given the right distribution, is a separate practical challenge.
A unit test is a degenerate case of a random test whose generator always returns the same input.

questions.query: How does Istio (service mesh) compare to Traefik (edge proxy)?

key_points.text: It is an apples-to-oranges comparison: edge proxies like Traefik or Nginx are best compared to Envoy, the proxy that Istio uses.
Istio automatically installs an Envoy proxy adjacent to every pod (sidecar).
Istio adds higher-level capabilities on top of Envoy: routing, ACLs, service discovery and access policy across a set of services.
Stitching a set of Envoy-enabled services together this way is the design pattern called a service mesh.

questions.query: How to use feature flag toggles in an application, step by step?

key_points.text: Feature flags are an engineering device to avoid long-lived branches and the conflicts they cause in product development.
First wrap the existing implementation behind an interface: rename it to a v1 class and add a delegate class implementing the shared interface that calls v1.
Then introduce a configuration flag that governs which implementation the delegate uses, with a v2 placeholder implementing the interface whose methods initially throw 'Not implemented'.

After this, developers working on old and new versions can collaborate on short-lived branches without explicit synchronisation because all code is bound by the shared interface, minimising conflicts.

questions.query: difference between blocking and nonblocking assignment in Verilog

key_points.text: A blocking assignment executes in series: it blocks execution of the next statement until it completes, so later statements can depend on its result.
Nonblocking assignments describe assignments that all occur at the same time; a later statement executes as if the earlier nonblocking assignment had not happened yet.
Continuous assign statements are neither blocking nor nonblocking; blocking/nonblocking assignments exist only inside always blocks.
A blocking assignment takes effect immediately when processed; a nonblocking assignment takes effect at the end of processing the current time delta.

Sequential logic (always @(posedge clk)) normally uses nonblocking assignments so the state after the clock edge is defined in terms of the state before it; combinational logic usually uses blocking assignments.

Do not mix blocking and nonblocking assignments to the same reg, and do not read a blocking-assigned variable of a sequential block from outside it, or simulation and synthesis may differ or synthesis may fail.
In synthesized logic 'blocking' does not mean time-sequential hardware: everything runs in parallel and an always_comb block settles to a stable state as the circuit does.

questions.query: why are inferred latches bad in Verilog

key_points.text: A variable not assigned in some path of an always block keeps its previous value, so synthesis creates a latch; incomplete if-else statements or case statements without a default infer latches.
An inferred latch is a warning sign that the logic is not implemented as intended, e.g. a missing if-else or case branch.
Latches can cause timing issues and race conditions, and may create unpredictable combinational feedback.
Many FPGAs have no built-in latch, so latches are built from logic gates, giving poor control over timing delays and races.
Avoid latches by covering all if/case branches, assigning every output in every branch, and using default assignments at the start of the block.
Intentional latches are justified only when truly needed, e.g. time borrowing to meet a required clock frequency.

questions.query: how is ASIC design different from FPGA HDL synthesis

key_points.text: ASIC design is a team effort following a multi-step flow: build/obtain a cell library, characterize it, synthesize, then place and route.

A cell library contains gates of multiple drive strengths, pad drivers and macros (multipliers, memories), each designed as a schematic and physical layout; commercial gate libraries can be bought instead.

Each cell is characterized by extracting layout parasitics and simulating under varying inputs and output loads to produce timing models (Liberty format) for static timing analysis, at worst/nominal/best corners.
Synthesis turns the high-level/RTL design into a gate-level netlist, giving the first view of performance and where drive-strength issues are addressed.

Because silicon costs a million dollars or more, ASIC teams spend far more effort on pre-silicon verification (simulator farms, emulators, extensive tests), whereas FPGA designers test largely in the target system.

questions.query: can an FPGA design be mostly or completely asynchronous

key_points.text: An FPGA can run a completely asynchronous design.
Timing through an FPGA is not very predictable and varies between place-and-route runs, so an asynchronous design can change behaviour with even slight design changes.
Maximum-delay constraints can be put on individual asynchronous paths, but a minimum delay may not be specifiable, so the whole timing report must be checked after every change.

With a synchronous design and proper constraints you just check pass/fail after place and route, so practitioners aim for fully synchronous designs (simple buffering/inversion can skip a flip-flop if constrained).
Entire asynchronous CPUs have been built; asynchronous design has theoretical advantages and is rejected mainly because tools support it poorly.
Globally asynchronous, locally synchronous (GALS) design gains some asynchronous advantages while staying mostly synchronous.

questions.query: test driven development TDD for logic chip design in Verilog or VHDL

key_points.text: TDD works for FPGA/HDL code: keep a full suite of tests for all functional code and try to write the test code first.
Staring at waveforms happens when debugging but is not a good way of validating code.
Testing in real hardware is hard (corner cases are hard to stimulate) and an HDL simulation compile takes seconds versus minutes or hours for a hardware build, so tests belong in simulation.
Designers can build assertions into the RTL as they write it to catch conditions that should never happen, not leaving assertions only to verification engineers.

VUnit, a Python library that invokes the VHDL compiler and simulator and reads the results, supports TDD with communication, logging and checking libraries and Python-side test data generation/checking.
A downside of VUnit is harder debugging of compilation errors due to many overloaded subprogram names and behind-the-scenes preprocessing.

questions.query: Can a local variable's memory be accessed outside its scope (returning address of a local)?

key_points.text: Dereferencing a pointer to a local after its function returns is undefined behaviour; it appears to work only by luck because nothing has yet overwritten that memory.
Locals are allocated on a stack because their lifetimes nest (last allocated, first freed), making allocation cheap; storage with unpredictable lifetimes goes to a heap manager.
The implementation is not required to zero or unmap the popped stack region, because doing so would be expensive, so the stale value usually remains readable.
A later function call pushes a new stack frame over the same addresses, so the old value changes and the dangling pointer can clobber unrelated locals.
Memory debuggers such as Valgrind detect such invalid accesses, and compilers like GCC warn that the address of a local variable is returned.
Memory-safe languages remove the problem by restricting power, e.g. C# forbids returning the address of a local outside an explicit unsafe mode.

questions.query: What does int 0x80 mean in x86 assembly code?

key_points.text: int is the software-interrupt instruction and 0x80 is the interrupt vector number; executing it transfers control to the handler registered for that vector.
On Linux the vector 0x80 handler is the kernel's system-call entry: the syscall number goes in EAX (e.g. 1 = exit, 4 = write) and arguments in EBX, ECX, EDX and further registers.
The CPU locates the handler through an interrupt vector table: in real mode the IVT of 4-byte entries at address 0, in protected mode the Interrupt Descriptor Table loaded with LIDT.
User programs run in ring 3 and cannot install their own interrupt handlers; Linux sets up the 0x80 handler so user code can request kernel services.
int 0x80 has been superseded by faster mechanisms: sysenter, the vDSO, and the syscall instruction on x86-64.
Software interrupts must not be confused with hardware interrupts; DOS used int 0x21 with function codes in AH/AL in the same way for its services.

questions.query: What is the difference between atomic, volatile and synchronized in Java and how do they work internally?

key_points.text: An unsynchronized counter++ is a read-modify-write that suffers both a race condition and visibility problems, since a value may sit in a core's cache (the thread's 'local copy') unseen by other threads.
volatile guarantees visibility of writes to other threads but not atomicity, so counter++ or i += 5 on a volatile field still races.
AtomicInteger uses low-level CPU compare-and-swap in a loop: read the value, try compareAndSet(current, current+1), and retry if another thread changed it, with no locking.
synchronized only excludes threads that lock the same object, so locking a changing object has no effect, and the lock must span the whole read-to-write sequence.
Atomicity, synchronization and volatility are independent attributes; synchronized lets only one thread at a time access the variable while others wait.

questions.query: How many files can I put in a directory on Linux and what are the impacts of too many?

key_points.text: Per-directory limits depend on the filesystem: FAT32 allows 65,535 files per directory, ext2 has performance issues past about 10,000, ext4 about 10 million (extendable with large_dir).
ext3 with dir_index (htree) hashing makes lookups in large directories fast; without it, directories with thousands of entries were slow to list and even to open a single file.
Listing huge directories with ls/find is slow because libc readdir() reads only 32K of directory entries at a time; calling getdents() directly with a larger buffer is faster.
With too many files the shell's wildcard expansion fails with 'Argument list too long'.
A common mitigation is sharding files into subdirectories keyed by digits of the id, using the last digits so the load is balanced.
Measurements differ: one user saw no penalty for random access to 1,000,000 files in an ext4 directory, another saw 200-400 ms vs 40 ms serving files from an 88,914-file directory.

questions.query: What is the status and purpose of POSIX asynchronous I/O (AIO) across Linux and BSD?

key_points.text: Socket I/O is already handled well by event mechanisms (epoll, kqueue, IOCP / non-blocking event loops), so POSIX AIO's real purpose is asynchronous disk I/O.
With AIO the kernel can order reads globally because it sees all disk I/O, may know head position and can use native command queuing; lio_listio can submit many reads per call.

The POSIX AIO interface is awkward: completion via signals uses the process-global signal namespace and is hard in libraries and threads, lio_suspend scales like select, and lio_listio limits are not portable.

Implementations differ: glibc's POSIX AIO emulates asynchrony with user-level threads, Linux's native io_submit interface is truly asynchronous down to the driver, and many OSes restrict AIO to regular files.
Writes are already buffered and reads can be prefetched with posix_fadvise, leaving direct unbuffered I/O for transactional databases as AIO's only real use, and those manage their own I/O threads.

questions.query: What is the meaning of char foo(|10|) in C on a z/OS mainframe

key_points.text: (| and |) are an early or non-standard digraph form standing in for the square brackets [ and ], so char foo(|10|) declares an array of 10 chars.
The code was probably written in EBCDIC, which does not have the [ ] characters in all code pages.
The SAS/C compiler for System/370 documents (| |) as alternate forms for [ ].
Standard C later added digraphs (<: :>) and trigraphs (??( ??)) to solve the same missing-character problem.

questions.query: What did code on punch cards do with the other six bits per column

key_points.text: Punch card codes were not binary numbers but hole-pattern (n-out-of-m) encodings using combinations of zero to three holes per column.
Digits used a single hole in rows 0-9; letters combined one zone punch (rows 12, 11, 0) with one digit punch in rows 1-9, giving 3 x 9 = 27 combinations for the 26 letters plus one extra.
Punctuation/special characters always punched row 8 plus a digit row 1-7, optionally with one zone hole, giving two- and three-hole patterns.
Using all holes in a column would weaken the card mechanically and jam card readers; cards with every hole punched were called lace cards.
The encoding line runs from Hollerith's decimal-based card code through to EBCDIC.

questions.query: Why were COBOL applications not ported from IBM mainframes to microcomputers

key_points.text: Few mainframe applications made sense on desktop micros: mainframe software is about data processing over company-wide repositories, not interactive computing.
Where whole applications did migrate downward, it was toward IBM /3x systems and ultimately AS/400, which was well supported and rather painless.
COBOL workloads need throughput: I/O-bound processing of large data volumes in a fixed time, which mainframes handle with dedicated I/O processor hardware that micros lack.
COBOL applications often cannot tolerate downtime or errors, and mainframes have built-in hardware and software redundancy that micros typically lack.
Older applications are not rewritten because they work as-is and rewriting risks changing behaviour and introducing new bugs.

questions.query: Why did 1950s-60s computers have such wide words

key_points.text: Early computers were built to automate numeric calculation, so word size was set by how many digits a number needs for meaningful calculation (about 10 decimal digits, 33-40 bits; ENIAC had 40).
Such words held more bits than one instruction needs, so several instructions were packed into a word or the instruction had a large address field.
Teletype characters were 6 bits, so word sizes in multiples of 6 (e.g. 36) made sense; DEC's 12-bit PDP-8 was a fraction of 36, and later machines moved to multiples of 8.
A wider word processes more bits per step; with slow electronics, widening the word was one of the few ways to improve performance, until the 1970s focus shifted to cost and 8-bit CPUs.
With very slow (drum) memory, wide registers let multi-digit arithmetic proceed without many intermediate memory accesses.

questions.query: What programming languages were most commonly used on the AS/400 in the 90s

key_points.text: RPG has been the dominant language on AS/400 / IBM i; today Java may rival it depending on whether new or in-use programs are counted.
COBOL is far behind RPG; PL/I was used for odd tasks RPG and COBOL struggled with, a role C gradually took over; other languages were minor.
IBM i is the operating system (successor of OS/400); current hardware is IBM Power Systems, which also run AIX and Linux, and PASE lets IBM i run AIX programs.

Under the Original Program Model one source file became one program with no Unix-like linking; EPM was a near-unusable first attempt at C, and ILE made the system more Unix-like, with Java needing further OS changes.

questions.query: How can building a heap be O(n) time complexity?

key_points.text: buildHeap runs in O(n) when it sifts nodes down starting from the end of the array (bottom-up heapify), because siftDown cost is proportional to a node's height and most nodes sit near the bottom of the tree.
The siftDown work is the sum (0*n/2)+(1*n/4)+(2*n/8)+...+(h*1), i.e. nodes per level times maximum distance moved; this series is bounded by a constant times n, so the total is O(n).
Building the heap by siftUp on each node / repeated insertion costs O(n log n), since the first term alone (h*n/2) is already (1/2) n log n.
Leaves (about half the nodes) need no work at all, nodes just above the leaves need at most one level of comparison, and only the root can need log n.

questions.query: What is the difference between likelihood and probability?

key_points.text: Probability P(O|theta) treats the parameters as fixed and is a function of the outcomes; the likelihood L(theta|O)=P(O|theta) is the same expression viewed as a function of the unknown parameters with the observed data held fixed.
Maximum likelihood estimation chooses the parameter value that maximizes the likelihood of the observed data.
The likelihood function does not obey the laws of probability (for example it is not bound to [0,1]); it is only proportional to the probability of the observed data.

Probability and statistics address inverse problems: probability reasons from an assumed parameter to the probability of a sample, while statistics starts from the observation and makes inference about the parameter.
For continuous data one cannot speak of the probability of the exact observation; the likelihood is then built from the probability density.
In Bayesian inference, Bayes' formula combines the prior with the likelihood to produce the posterior.

questions.query: When should I use Kruskal as opposed to Prim (and vice versa)?

key_points.text: Use Kruskal when the graph is sparse (E=O(V)) or when edges are already sorted or sortable in linear time; use Prim when the graph is dense (E=O(V^2)).
Kruskal is O(E log E) because it sorts the edges; Prim is O(E log V) with a binary-heap priority queue, or O(E + V log V) with a Fibonacci heap.

Kruskal grows the solution from the cheapest edge, repeatedly adding the next cheapest edge that does not create a cycle; Prim grows from a start vertex, repeatedly adding the vertex connected to the tree by the cheapest edge.
In their optimal forms Kruskal uses union-find and Prim a Fibonacci heap; Kruskal is easier to implement, while Prim with a Fibonacci heap needs bookkeeping linking graph nodes and heap nodes.
With multiple processing units Boruvka's algorithm should be considered because it parallelizes easily.
Stopped midway, Prim always holds a connected tree while Kruskal may hold a disconnected forest.

questions.query: When should I use Gini impurity as opposed to information gain (entropy) in decision trees?

key_points.text: Gini impurity and entropy-based information gain are practically interchangeable; the choice affects results in only about 2% of cases (Raileanu and Stoffel).
Gini(E) = 1 - sum p_j^2 and entropy H(E) = -sum p_j log p_j.
Gini is cheaper to compute because it needs no logarithm, so it is a reasonable default.
For a two-class variable, Gini 2f(1-f) and entropy scaled by ln 2 give nearly identical curves when normalized.
Gini is more suited to minimizing misclassification, while entropy penalizes small probabilities more.

questions.query: Why is the Halting Problem so important?

key_points.text: Many practical problems (optimal compilation, information-flow security, parser equivalence, antivirus detection) are the halting problem in disguise: solving them would solve halting.

The halting problem is a well-defined specification, not a paradox: halts(P,x) has a definite value for every pair; what is impossible is one program deciding it for all pairs, and the self-referential program is only the proof technique.
Treating a real computer as a finite-state machine is impractical: n bits of memory give 2^n states, and halting for a finite machine can only be decided by a bigger machine.
Rice's theorem: any non-trivial property of what a Turing machine accepts is undecidable.
Undecidability ended the search for Hilbert's algorithm that decides all theorems; it is connected to Godel's incompleteness and to Hilbert's tenth problem on Diophantine equations.
In practice one falls back on heuristics and second-best methods, or uses languages that are not Turing-complete (no unbounded recursion or iteration) so they can be analyzed.
The busy beaver function has a well-defined value for every n, yet no program can compute it.

questions.query: A monad is just a monoid in the category of endofunctors, what's the problem?

key_points.text: The phrasing is James Iry's joke (fictionally attributed to Wadler); the original is Saunders Mac Lane's Categories for the Working Mathematician: a monad in X is a monoid in the category of endofunctors of X, with product replaced by composition of endofunctors and unit by the identity endofunctor.
A monad is an endofunctor T: X -> X with natural transformations mu: T o T -> T (join) and eta: I -> T (return) satisfying associativity and unit laws.
A monoid is a set with an associative binary operation and an identity element; the monad laws are the same abstract shape with functor composition in place of the product.
In the category of endofunctors on X, the objects are endofunctors and the morphisms are natural transformations.
In Haskell every Functor is an endofunctor on the category of Haskell types and functions, and a natural transformation is a polymorphic function f x -> g x that cannot inspect the type parameter.
The statement must be read as a monoid object in a monoidal category (endofunctors with composition as tensor and identity as unit), not as a monoid formed by a set of endofunctors.

questions.query: What is the difference between px, dip, dp, and sp in Android?

key_points.text: dp (dip, density-independent pixel) is an abstract unit based on the physical density of the screen, relative to a 160 dpi baseline: one dp equals one physical pixel on a 160 dpi screen.
sp (scale-independent pixel) is like dp but is also scaled by the user's font size preference, so it is the recommended unit for font sizes.
px corresponds to actual screen pixels, while in, mm and pt (1/72 inch) are based on the physical size of the screen.
The conversion is px = dp * (dpi / 160); for example on a 240 dpi screen 1 dp equals 1.5 physical pixels, and the system scales dp units at runtime.

Android groups screens into generalized density buckets (ldpi 120, mdpi 160, hdpi 240, xhdpi 320, xxhdpi 480, xxxhdpi 640 dpi), so a bitmap of a given dp size must be supplied at different pixel sizes per bucket (e.g. 100x100 px mdpi, 150x150 hdpi, 200x200 xhdpi).
Layouts should be defined in dp so they display correctly across densities; apps should reason about generalized screen size and density rather than raw resolution.

questions.query: How to fix android.os.NetworkOnMainThreadException?

key_points.text: NetworkOnMainThreadException is thrown when an app performs a networking operation on its main thread; the fix is to run the network code on a background thread or asynchronous task (e.g. AsyncTask doInBackground with results delivered in onPostExecute).

The restriction can be switched off with a permissive StrictMode ThreadPolicy, but then on spotty connections the app becomes unresponsive and locks up, users force-kill it, and the activity manager may kill the app.

AsyncTasks created as non-static inner classes hold an implicit reference to the enclosing Activity and its view hierarchy, preventing garbage collection until the work completes, which causes short-term memory leaks, e.g. across repeated orientation changes.

AsyncTask execution characteristics differ by API level (serial on one background thread, then a pool of up to 128 threads, then serial again from API 11 unless executeOnExecutor is used), so code with hidden ordering dependencies can break across platforms.

More robust alternatives are a networking library or a Service/IntentService that returns results (e.g. via PendingIntent); the system is less likely to kill an app with an active Service, so in-flight work survives activity restarts.
Network access also requires declaring the android.permission.INTERNET permission in the manifest.

questions.query: Is there a unique Android device ID?

key_points.text: Settings.Secure.ANDROID_ID returns a 64-bit hex string and is the preferred device identifier, but it can change on factory reset and on Android 2.2 a bug made many devices share the same value (9774d56d682e549c).

Telephony identifiers such as TelephonyManager.getDeviceId (IMEI/MEID) and the SIM serial only work on some devices (e.g. SIM serial is null on CDMA) and require the READ_PHONE_STATE permission, which users find suspicious; identifiers can be hashed so they are not explicitly the device's real ID.

Hardware-based identifiers are suited to tracking hardware, not users; users change devices and can alter IDs on rooted devices, so tracking an individual user is best done (with consent) by having them log in.

Hardware identifiers (IMEI, MAC, serial) are unreliable and increasingly inaccessible because of stricter runtime permissions and security fixes (e.g. CVE-2018-9489 for Wi-Fi based techniques); official guidance is to avoid them.
The Advertising ID is only for ads/profiling and users can reset or block it, so it is not a device identifier either.

The recommended approach is an installation identifier: generate a random UUID (or Firebase installation ID) on first run and store it privately (e.g. SharedPreferences); it identifies the app install and is lost on uninstall unless backed up.

questions.query: What's the difference between the atomic and nonatomic property attributes in Objective-C?

key_points.text: atomic is the default; with synthesized accessors it guarantees that a whole, viable value is always returned by the getter or stored by the setter regardless of concurrent setter activity on other threads, while nonatomic gives no such guarantee and is considerably faster.

atomic does not make an object thread-safe: with concurrent setters a reader may get any of the values, and other messages sent to the object (e.g. release from another thread) are not protected at all.

Atomicity of individual properties cannot keep multiple dependent properties consistent (e.g. firstName/lastName read via fullName mid-update); that requires a transactional model with other synchronization or exclusion.

The atomic accessors take a lock and retain/autorelease the returned object so it stays alive for the caller even if another thread replaces it; the real implementation uses object-level spin locks rather than @synchronized(self).
Atomic access can be very fast when uncontended, but in less ideal cases costs more than 20 times nonatomic, and a contested 7-thread case measured 44 times slower; ARC vs MRC also changes the cost.

questions.query: Pros and cons of React vs Web Components (Polymer)

key_points.text: React and Web Components solve different problems: Web Components provide strong encapsulation for reusable components, while React is a declarative library that keeps the DOM in sync with data; they are complementary and can be mixed (React inside Web Components or vice versa).

Polymer is a library for building backwards-compatible web components, whereas React is only the View layer, not a framework; the two overlap in defining components but are otherwise very different tools.
The 'markup in HTML, styles in CSS' objection is weak: HTML is a good DSL for static documents but offers nothing for dynamic HTML, and JavaScript is the best way to make HTML and CSS dynamic.
React's biggest drawback is that it is not based on web standards and circumvents browser facilities, so its design choices may stop making sense as built-in browser capabilities improve.

The virtual DOM is overhead on top of the real DOM (a React div plus a native div, not instead of one); in the answerer's measurements React was not faster than well-written Backbone/Polymer apps and a React rewrite used about 30% more memory than the Polymer version.

questions.query: What is the mask in a WebSocket frame and why is it required?

key_points.text: Client-to-server masking exists to prevent cache-poisoning attacks on proxies/intermediaries: because the browser picks a random mask per frame, hostile script cannot choose the byte patterns that appear on the wire (RFC 6455 section 10.3).
The payload is XORed with a random 32-bit masking key, and the unpredictability of the masking key is essential (RFC 6455 section 5.3).
Masking of client frames is obligatory, not merely recommended.

The attack: an intermediary (e.g. a transparent proxy) that does not understand WebSocket treats the upgraded connection as HTTP, so injected bytes that look like an HTTP request with a forged Host header get routed/cached, poisoning the cache (Huang et al., 'Talking to Yourself for Fun and Profit', W2SP 2011).
The browser, not the JavaScript code, chooses the mask, so even attackers controlling both the page script and the server cannot predict the final byte stream.
Masking is redundant when the WebSocket stream is encrypted with TLS.

questions.query: What is the largest safe UDP packet size on the Internet?

key_points.text: The maximum safe IPv4 UDP payload is 508 bytes: the 576-byte minimum reassembly buffer minus a maximum 60-byte IP header minus the 8-byte UDP header; anything larger may be dropped by any router.

IP options can grow the IP header to as much as 60 bytes, and intermediate nodes may encapsulate datagrams (e.g. IPsec/VPN), so leave margin when the path MTU is unknown; a 512-byte payload is the conventional choice.
576 bytes is the minimum maximum reassembly buffer size (EMTU_R): every IPv4 host must be able to reassemble datagrams of at least that size (RFC 1122, RFC 791).
On an IPv6-only route the safe maximum payload is larger (1,212 bytes).
Any UDP datagram may be fragmented; losing one fragment loses the whole datagram, which has the same effect as losing an unfragmented packet.
The theoretical maximum UDP payload is 65,507 bytes = 65,535 - (20-byte IP header + 8-byte UDP header), but most protocols limit themselves far below it.

questions.query: Why use iBGP inside an autonomous system if IGP protocols like OSPF handle internal routing?

key_points.text: Scalability: BGP can carry far more routes (e.g. the full Internet table of ~500,000 routes) than an IGP; you use iBGP so you do not have to carry the Internet routing table in OSPF, whose LSA flooding/processing would overwhelm routers.
BGP has richer filtering for enforcing boundaries of trust and control over what is advertised and received.
BGP attributes such as communities, extended communities and local-pref let you implement custom routing policy inside your AS, e.g. influencing the per-route exit point.
Trade-off: iBGP generally converges more slowly than IGPs.

IGPs like OSPF/IS-IS are link-state, giving every router a full topology view that enables fast convergence and traffic engineering, while BGP is essentially distance-vector with a limited view; link-state is too expensive to scale to Internet DFZ size.
Keep the IGP small (core router loopbacks) and carry customer/Internet prefixes in BGP; redistributing BGP into the IGP hurts IGP performance and has caused major ISP outages.

questions.query: What does "connection reset by peer" mean on a TCP connection?

key_points.text: The remote side sent a TCP RST and the connection is now closed; it is a fatal error for that connection.
An RST drops the connection immediately instead of the normal FIN handshake, bypassing the half-closed state transitions.
An RST is sent when a segment arrives for a connection the other end does not recognize, e.g. after the peer crashed and came back up.
It also happens when the peer calls close() while data from you is still in transit, signalling that some data you sent may not have been received.
Whether it is an application error depends on the protocol, but you should close the socket and free associated resources.

questions.query: TCP: can two different sockets share a port?

key_points.text: A TCP connection is uniquely identified by the tuple (local IP, local port, remote IP, remote port[, protocol]); many connections can share the same server-side IP/port as long as the client-side IP/port pairs differ.
A connected socket is not assigned a new dedicated port; that is a common but incorrect intuition.
A server listens on one port; when a connection arrives it is handed off to a separate connected socket/thread, so communication never hogs the listening port.
The client picks a random unused (ephemeral) source port for each outbound connection, so the client side can run out of ports when opening many connections quickly.
A server can handle as many clients as available system resources allow, not a 64K port limit.

questions.query: What is anycast and how is it helpful?

key_points.text: Anycast advertises the same IP prefix from multiple locations, and the network (routing protocol costs, BGP) delivers each user to the 'closest' location.
Users reach the nearest instance, reducing latency and providing a degree of load balancing.
Configuration is simpler: one IP address (e.g. for DNS servers) is configured everywhere instead of per-region addresses.
If the route advertisement is conditional on a health check, a failed server's route is withdrawn and, after reconvergence, requests go to the next-closest instance automatically (high availability).
It supports horizontal scaling: deploy another instance near an overloaded one and it takes part of the load with no client reconfiguration.
It is mainly used for UDP-based services such as DNS, and 'closest' means best by BGP routing, not geography, so it is not guaranteed.

questions.query: Simulator or emulator: what is the difference?

key_points.text: Emulation mimics the outwardly observable behaviour of a target; the emulator's internal state need not reflect the target's internal state.
Simulation models the underlying internal state and components of the target, so one can look inside the simulation and observe properties the real target would show.
An emulator can substitute for the original in real use, whereas a simulator is a model built for study and analysis.
An emulator has to run close to real time, while a simulation may run far slower or far faster than real time.
In practice simulations take performance shortcuts, so some internal aspects of a simulation may themselves be emulated.

questions.query: What is a Mathematica packed array, and when is packed vs unpacked faster or smaller?

key_points.text: A packed array stores its elements in a direct C-style contiguous block of memory, whereas an unpacked array holds an array of pointers to its elements.
Packed arrays are much more space efficient because all elements share one type, so no per-element type information is stored (about 4x smaller in the example).
Most of the speed-up comes from built-in (Listable numeric) functions that have specialized low-level implementations for packed arrays, acting as a partial replacement for compilation.

Many operations silently unpack an array (e.g. Select, assigning an element of a different type, Listable pure functions, downvalues), which explains mysterious slowdowns; vectorized code or compiled functions keep data packed.
Packed arrays are not faster for everything: accessing a single element was about twice as slow and appending was no faster.
The restriction to rectangular, homogeneous arrays allows allocation as one contiguous block and fast bulk copying.

questions.query: MPICH vs Open MPI: differences between the two MPI implementations

key_points.text: MPICH aims to be a high-quality reference implementation of the latest MPI standard and the basis for derivative implementations (MVAPICH, Intel MPI, Cray MPI), while Open MPI targets the common case in usage and network conduits.

MPICH has been first to implement each MPI standard release and has long had holistic MPI_THREAD_MULTIPLE support; Open MPI historically lacked general MPI_THREAD_MULTIPLE support and had broken one-sided (RMA) communication in 1.x.

Both support many networks via OFI/libfabric; Open MPI also supports networks such as InfiniBand natively, while MPICH reaches InfiniBand and proprietary interconnects (Cray, Blue Gene) through its derivatives.

MPICH and its derivatives keep ABI compatibility, so a binary compiled against one can run with another; Open MPI does not promise ABI compatibility but invests in launcher compatibility for containers.
MPICH's old MPD process manager was brittle but was replaced by Hydra, which is comparable to Open MPI's ORTE launcher.

Both are standards-compliant; on a production cluster benchmark your application on both against your network, with MPICH often preferred for development/debugging and Open MPI often faster in production.

questions.query: Why does collecting data until finding a significant result increase the Type I error rate?

key_points.text: Testing repeatedly as data arrive and stopping at the first significant result gives yourself too many chances to pass the test, so the overall false-rejection rate exceeds the nominal level.

A fixed-n z-test rejects exactly 5% of the time for any fixed n, but the sequential procedure is a random walk S_n checked against a parabolic boundary |S_n| >= 1.96*sqrt(n), and a random walk very likely hits that boundary eventually if you wait long enough.

Under the null hypothesis the p-value is uniformly distributed and bounces around as data are added; it does not keep falling once below .05, so with enough tests it will eventually cross .05 (shown by simulation).

The test statistic behaves like Brownian motion; rescaled on log time it becomes an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process with constant barriers whose first-passage time is approximately exponential, so the probability of eventually reaching significance tends to one.

questions.query: Can a Turing machine simulate a quantum computer?

key_points.text: Yes: a classical Turing machine can simulate a quantum computer, so whatever a quantum computer can compute a Turing machine can compute by simulating it.

Quantum advantage is about efficiency, not computability: superposition gives massive parallelism and efficiency gains that can be astronomically large, making simulation impractical on classical hardware though possible.
The randomness of measurement (wave-function collapse) needs a source of randomness, i.e. a probabilistic Turing machine, or can be captured with distribution mathematics.
Deutsch's 1985 paper argues a classical Turing machine cannot truly reproduce genuinely random outputs with quantum correlations; the answer depends on how 'simulate' is defined.

questions.query: Why are elementwise additions much faster in separate loops than in a combined loop?

key_points.text: Large separately allocated arrays get fresh pages from the OS, so they tend to sit at the same offset from a page boundary; this alignment is the main cause of the combined loop's slowdown.
With identical alignment all accesses in the loop fall on the same cache set/way, causing cache bank/way conflicts; even with 8-way L1 associativity, touching 4 ways is slower than 2.
The alignment most likely causes false (partial address) aliasing stalls in the load/store units; packing the arrays contiguously to break the alignment makes the single loop fast again.

Performance depends on working-set size versus cache sizes: tiny sizes are dominated by loop/branch overhead, beyond L1 performance is capped by L1-L2 bandwidth, and when nothing fits in cache it is bound by memory bandwidth.
The combined loop alternates between distant memory streams and generates more cache activity/misses, while each separate loop streams through adjacent addresses.

questions.query: How do I write a correct micro-benchmark in Java?

key_points.text: Always include a warm-up phase that runs the test kernel enough to trigger class initialization and JIT compilation before timing starts.
Run with -XX:+PrintCompilation and -verbose:gc to verify that the compiler and GC are not doing unexpected work during the timing phase; be aware of OSR versus regular compilation.
Beware deoptimization/recompilation and class-loading effects: do not take a code path or load classes for the first time inside the timing phase.
Use the results computed by the benchmarked code, otherwise the optimizer can eliminate the code entirely.
Reduce noise: run on a quiet machine for long enough, repeat runs (in fresh JVMs), discard outliers or take the median, and control GC effects.
Use a dedicated harness such as JMH or Caliper rather than a hand-rolled stopwatch loop.
Measure time per iteration if you care about latency and iterations per time if you care about throughput.

questions.query: What algorithm can be used for packing rectangles of different sizes into the smallest rectangle possible?

key_points.text: Packing rectangles optimally is NP-hard; exact solutions need backtracking search, which can prune many placements early.

Level-oriented strip-packing heuristics sort by non-increasing height and fill levels: NFDH (asymptotic ratio 2) and FFDH (asymptotic ratio 17/10) run in O(n log n); BFDH picks the level with least residual space.
The Bottom-Left heuristic places each item as low and then as far left as it fits (Chazelle's bottom-left packing); BL runs in O(n^2) with ratio at most 3·OPT.
More elaborate algorithms trade implementation complexity for better bounds: Baker's Up-Down (asymptotic 5/4), Split-Fit (3/2), Steinberg and Reverse-Fit (2), Sleator (2.5).
A simple greedy baseline places rectangles from largest to smallest, each where it extends the packed region the least.

For the optimal enclosing box, iterate candidate bounding boxes from smallest upward (e.g. powers of two) and use a decision procedure (Huang's algorithm) that answers whether the rectangles fit; the first yes is optimal, and rotations are tried with backtracking.
The problem is a case of two-dimensional bin packing, so the packing-problem literature applies.

questions.query: Why is NoSQL better at scaling out than RDBMS?

key_points.text: RDBMSs guarantee ACID transactions and strong consistency, which requires communication/synchronization between nodes for every transaction; this limits scale-out, so typically there is one master writer and several read slaves.

NoSQL systems trade strong consistency for eventual consistency, decoupling storing data from making it visible, so a transaction need not wait for inter-node communication and many nodes can be used.
NoSQL stores usually offer only record-level atomicity and cannot guarantee that a series of operations succeeds as a transaction.
The real advantage is horizontal scaling (sharding): self-contained documents can live on one server without joining rows held on other servers, whereas relational joins across shards are hard.

For many-to-one and many-to-many relationships any sharded database must look across nodes, so document locality only helps one-to-many data; nothing intrinsic in the relational model prevents horizontal scaling, NoSQL products just ship built-in sharding and routing.

questions.query: How do I profile C++ code running on Linux?

key_points.text: Valgrind's callgrind tool records a callgrind.out profile that kcachegrind visualises with per-line/per-function costs; the Self column separates a function's own time from its callees.

Valgrind is a virtual machine that JIT-translates the program into a processor-neutral IR and back; callgrind is non-probing, so even short runs give reliable results, and Massif profiles heap usage over time.
gprof requires recompiling with -pg instrumentation and combines instrumentation with sampling, balancing accuracy against slowdown.
Linux perf (perf_events) provides sampling profilers that can profile the whole system, showing interactions between threads, processes and the kernel.
The tools trade recompilation and slowdown: gprof needs recompilation with little slowdown, perf needs no recompilation and little slowdown, Valgrind needs no recompilation but is many times slower.
gprof has limitations: it does not handle multi-threaded code properly and its call graph is confused by function pointers.

questions.query: What does the yield keyword do in Python?

key_points.text: Calling a function whose body contains yield does not run the body; it returns a generator object.

Each time the generator is iterated, the body runs from where it last left off until it hits the next yield, whose value is returned; the generator is exhausted when the function runs to its end without hitting yield.
Generators are iterators that can be iterated only once: they compute values on the fly instead of storing them all in memory, which suits large sequences read once.
Iteration rests on iterables (implementing __iter__) and iterators (implementing __next__); a generator implements the iterator side.
Once a generator is exhausted it keeps raising StopIteration even if the conditions that ended it change; a new generator must be created.

questions.query: How do JavaScript closures work?

key_points.text: A closure is a function paired with a reference to its outer scope (lexical environment); every JavaScript function keeps a link to the lexical environment where it was declared.
A lexical environment maps identifiers to values; the chain of references to outer environments forms the scope chain used to resolve variables.
Code inside the function can see variables declared outside it regardless of when and where the function is later called, even after the outer function has returned.
Closed-over variables act as a private box of state reachable only through the function, giving data hiding and encapsulation.
A function does not have to be returned to form a closure; the captured variables persist and can be mutated across calls (e.g., a counter incremented on each call).

questions.query: Is < faster than <= ?

key_points.text: No: on x86 an integer comparison compiles to a cmp/test that sets EFLAGS plus one conditional jump (Jcc), so < and <= differ only in which jump (e.g. jg vs jge) is used, and these take the same time.

Intel documentation groups all Jcc instructions together with identical latency/throughput; when the branch is predicted correctly its latency is effectively zero, so branch predictability matters, not the condition tested.

For integers the two are semantically interchangeable; compilers adjust constants (a < 901 becomes a comparison against 900) and emit the same code, so a speed difference would indicate a broken compiler.
The same holds for floating point: an x87 compare sets the flags and seta/setae (or equivalent) tests them at equal cost.

questions.query: What is the Rule of Three in C++?

key_points.text: If a class needs a user-defined copy constructor, copy assignment operator, or destructor, it almost certainly needs all three.
The reason is resource management: a class that acquires a resource (e.g. in its constructor) and releases it in its destructor must also define what copying that resource means.
The implicitly defined copy constructor and assignment perform memberwise copy and the implicit destructor does nothing, which is correct when members manage themselves (e.g. std::string).

With a raw owning pointer member the default copy copies only the pointer, so two objects share memory; when one destructor deletes it the other holds a dangling pointer (double free / corruption), so a deep-copying copy constructor and assignment are needed.
If copying the resource has no sensible meaning, forbid copying by declaring (not defining) the copy constructor and assignment operator private.
C++11 move semantics extend the rule (move constructor and move assignment).

questions.query: How can I create a memory leak in Java?

key_points.text: A true Java leak is objects that running code can no longer use but that remain strongly reachable and so are never garbage collected.

ThreadLocal leak: a thread's threadLocals map holds weak keys but strong values, so a value that (via its class's static field) references its own ThreadLocal key is never collected while the thread lives; long-lived pooled threads make it worse.
Classloader leak: a leaked instance keeps its class, which keeps its ClassLoader and every class it loaded (especially bad in older JVMs with PermGen).
Static fields holding object references (e.g. a static collection) keep everything they reference alive.
Unclosed streams/connections and memory allocated through native methods that the garbage collector cannot reach also leak.
Using objects with missing or incorrect hashCode()/equals() as HashSet/HashMap keys makes 'duplicates' accumulate and become unremovable.

questions.query: What part of Hindley-Milner do you not understand? (reading the type inference rules)

key_points.text: Hindley-Milner is a set of inference rules showing that the most general type of a program can be deduced from its construction without explicit type declarations.
Notation: Γ is the environment (set of assumptions x : σ); ⊢ means 'from Γ we can deduce/assert'; e : σ means expression e has type σ.
In each rule the part above the horizontal line is the premise(s) and the part below is the conclusion.
Application and abstraction rules: if e0 : τ→τ' and e1 : τ then e0 e1 : τ'; if Γ extended with x : τ gives e : τ' then λx.e : τ→τ'.
Instantiation and generalization: a term of a more general type scheme can be used at a more specific instance (⊑); if e : σ and α is not free in Γ then e : ∀α.σ.
The let rule types let x = e0 in e1 by typing e1 with x bound to the (polymorphic) type of e0.

questions.query: Why can't I store a value and a reference to that value in the same struct in Rust?

key_points.text: Putting a value and a reference to it into the same struct is rejected by the borrow checker (cannot return value referencing local / cannot move out because it is borrowed).
Moving a value changes its memory address; a reference into it would keep pointing at the old location, which other code may reuse, causing crashes or security bugs.
Lifetimes exist to prevent exactly this: a value may not be moved while it is borrowed.

The same problem appears with lifetime-dependent objects (e.g. an ssh2 Session and its Channel); workarounds are keeping the owner outside the struct or crates such as owning_ref/rental that heap-allocate the owner in a Box so it does not move.

questions.query: Technically, why are processes in Erlang more efficient than OS threads?

key_points.text: Erlang processes are not OS processes or threads: they are lightweight (green) threads created and scheduled by the Erlang VM.
Context switches are cheap because processes switch only at known, controlled points, so the full CPU state (FPU/SSE registers, address-space mapping) need not be saved.
Each process starts with a very small, dynamically allocated stack that grows as needed, so millions of processes fit in memory.
With SMP the VM keeps separate run queues per core, and interaction between processes on the same scheduler stays lightweight.

Switching between coroutine-style processes takes on the order of tens of instructions/nanoseconds, whereas an OS thread switch costs hundreds of nanoseconds because it enters the kernel and its scheduler.
OS threads buy OS-enforced isolation and independent scheduling on cores; Erlang multiplexes many processes onto a pool of OS threads sized to the cores.

questions.query: Is Fortran easier to optimize than C for heavy calculations?

key_points.text: Fortran's speed advantage comes from aliasing: Fortran does not allow arguments/arrays to alias, so the compiler may assume they do not overlap.
In C any write through one pointer might change data seen through another, so the compiler must reload values (e.g. matrix elements) from memory instead of keeping them in registers.
C99 added the restrict qualifier (and strict-aliasing rules) so programmers can promise no aliasing and recover the optimization.
