In theory modern Fortran has no intrinsic advantage; in practice its edge comes from a language historically restricted to aid optimization and a culture of optimizing numerical code.
Fortran's whole-array operations (matmul, sum) and FORALL/PURE/ELEMENTAL constructs help compilers optimize and parallelize.

questions.query: What makes Lisp macros so special?

key_points.text: A Lisp macro is code that transforms code: it takes code as input and returns code that replaces the macro call before evaluation/compilation.
Macros let programmers extend the language's syntactic primitives and embed domain-specific languages (e.g. adding list-comprehension-like syntax).
Unlike macros in most languages, which work on text without the parser, Lisp macros receive preparsed source as lists because Lisp source is list data, so they manipulate code reliably.
Example: setf is a macro that inspects its first argument, such as (car x), and rewrites the form into the right primitive (rplaca) at compile time.
In C a macro cannot, for example, extend switch to strings; you would need a custom preprocessor.

questions.query: Why can the discrete Fourier transform be implemented efficiently as a quantum circuit?

key_points.text: The QFT can be realised efficiently because of the structure of its coefficients: it can be written as a quadratic form expansion, a sum over paths whose phases are a quadratic function of the input and output bits.

That structure maps onto a circuit of Hadamard gates linking each input wire to an output wire, SWAP gates for the bit-order reversal, and otherwise only two-qubit controlled-phase gates that admit a well-defined time ordering.
The DFT matrix has mutually orthogonal columns of unit magnitude, i.e. it is unitary, so it is a valid quantum operation.
Computed directly, the classical DFT costs O(N^2) operations (N operations per output element); the fast Fourier transform reduces this by exploiting the symmetry of the Fourier matrix.

questions.query: What kinds of problems can be solved more efficiently using a quantum computer? Is there a general statement?

key_points.text: There is no precise general statement of which problems quantum computers speed up; the question is as hard as asking where randomised algorithms help classically, which for super-polynomial advantage is the open P vs BPP question.
The class of problems efficiently solvable by quantum computers is BQP (bounded-error quantum polynomial time), the quantum counterpart of BPP.
BQP is contained in P^#P and hence in PSPACE; it is suspected to be a strict superset of P and disjoint from the NP-complete problems, but neither is proven.
Integer factorization and discrete log are in BQP; both are NP problems suspected to lie outside BPP and not to be NP-complete.
It is a misconception that quantum computers solve NP-complete problems in polynomial time; quantum speedups have rigid upper bounds, e.g. Grover's algorithm is optimal for unstructured search.

questions.query: Are there emulators for quantum computers that run on a classical computer?

key_points.text: Emulating or simulating a quantum computer on a classical computer is possible, but it is slow and inefficient for large numbers of qubits.

The cost grows exponentially: the state space has dimension 2^n for n qubits, so the linear algebra involves very large matrices and many classical bits are needed per qubit; cost can also grow with circuit depth and particular operation counts.
There is an accuracy trade-off: more accurate emulators use significantly more memory and run slower, and reducing accuracy allows more qubits in the same memory.
Emulators can use alternative state representations, e.g. QDD represents the quantum state with Binary Decision Diagrams.
Q# ships bundled with Microsoft's own simulator in the Quantum Development Kit, so Q# programs run on the emulator by default.

questions.query: Was the reduction from factoring to order-finding in Shor's algorithm originally discovered by Shor?

key_points.text: Shor discovered or rediscovered the reduction of factoring to order-finding himself, having found the discrete log algorithm first and knowing from it that periodicity was useful.
The reduction rests on the fact that factoring N is equivalent to finding two unequal numbers with equal squares mod N, which is also the basis of the quadratic sieve.

The randomized reduction from factoring to order-finding mod N was well known to number-theory algorithm researchers in the late 1970s and early 1980s and appears in Heather Woll's 'Reductions among number theoretic problems' (1987).
A closely similar, earlier-known result is the reduction of factoring to computing the Euler phi function.
Order-finding modulo N is equivalent to factoring N; order-finding is provably exponential classically only in an oracle setting.

questions.query: shards and replicas in Elasticsearch

key_points.text: An index is split into primary shards that hold the data itself (not copies); each document belongs to exactly one primary shard, and shards are spread across the cluster's nodes so the index can scale beyond one machine.
A replica shard is a copy of a primary shard, used for fail-over and to increase search performance.
A replica is never allocated on the same node as its primary, so a single-node cluster leaves replicas unassigned.
If a node fails, replicas of its primaries are promoted to primaries; with replicas unassigned the cluster is YELLOW (no data lost) until the node returns and replicas are resynchronised to GREEN.
The number of primary shards is fixed at index creation (changing it requires reindexing), while the number of replicas can be changed dynamically at any time.
Every shard has a cost, so with a single node and no foreseeable growth a single primary shard is advisable.

questions.query: difference between Lucene and Elasticsearch

key_points.text: Lucene is a Java search library you embed via function calls; Elasticsearch is a standalone JSON/REST-based search server built on top of Lucene, which does the actual indexing and search work underneath.
Each Elasticsearch shard is a separate Lucene instance/index; an Elasticsearch index is a collection of such shards.
Elasticsearch adds a distributed system (sharding, replication for high availability, cluster management) that Lucene is not aware of or built for.
Elasticsearch adds a JSON query DSL so complex queries can be written without Lucene syntax, plus aggregations and monitoring/management APIs.
A Lucene index is an inverted index: a term dictionary mapping each term to the documents containing it, with term frequencies, which makes term-based search efficient.
Elasticsearch is schema-free: it can create field mappings automatically at index time.

questions.query: metrics for evaluating ranking algorithms advantages and disadvantages MAP NDCG MRR Kendall tau

key_points.text: Each ranking metric has different traits, and which to use depends on what you actually want to measure.
Spearman's rho penalises errors at the top of the list with the same weight as at the bottom, so it is usually not the metric for evaluating rankings.
DCG/NDCG support non-binary (graded) relevance with fixed position discounts, and NDCG is usually preferred because it normalises DCG.
NDCG should be computed at a fixed cutoff @k because a long tail of irrelevant results biases it, while MAP is the classic standard metric in the field.
Mean Reciprocal Rank only reflects the position of the first relevant document, so it is unsuitable when many relevant documents should rank high.
When only the top k results matter, top-k accuracy, precision@k (relevant items in top k divided by k) and recall@k are appropriate metrics.

questions.query: better similarity ranking algorithm for variable length strings

key_points.text: Comparing adjacent character pairs (letter bigrams) of the two strings, as in Simon White's Strike-a-Match algorithm, works well for variable-length strings.
Similarity is computed as 2 x (number of shared pairs) / (total pairs in both strings), giving a value from 0 to 1.
A matched pair must be removed from the second list so that repeated pairs (e.g. 'GGGG' vs 'GG') are not over-counted as a full match.
The method reflects substring overlap, is robust to changes of word order, still treats random anagrams as dissimilar, and is language independent.
Strings are case-normalised and split into words, and letter pairs are taken within each word (pairs containing spaces are discarded).
The technique is a known algorithm, shingling, first presented by Digital Equipment Corporation.

questions.query: how does DuckDuckGo know my native language even though I use a VPN in another country

key_points.text: The site can choose the display language from request headers, especially the Accept-Language header, without any tracking.
Browsers send Accept-Language by default, derived from the user's browser language preference settings.
An IPv6 leak can bypass the VPN so the service sees the real home IP; blocking IPv6 made Google respond in the VPN country's language.
The browser language is also exposed to JavaScript via navigator.language.

questions.query: XKCD 936: short complex password or long dictionary passphrase?

key_points.text: A strong password policy must balance two equally important aspects: difficulty to guess (the computer aspect) and difficulty to remember (the human aspect), and the human aspect is often overriding.
Strict complexity rules push users to write passwords down (e.g. a sticky note on the screen) or choose predictable patterns, so security at the expense of usability comes at the expense of security.

Password strength should be measured as the entropy (in bits) of the generation process, assuming the attacker knows the method; n bits means about 2^(n-1) guesses on average, and bits of independent choices add up.

The passphrase method draws several words uniformly and independently at random from a public word list (e.g. Diceware's 7776 words, about 12.9 bits per word); strength comes from the random choice, not from secrecy of the list.
Passphrase entropy depends on word-list size and number of words, not character count, and the words must be random: human-chosen phrases or well-known sentences sharply reduce entropy.
Common tweaks such as leet-speak substitutions, capitalization and appended digits/punctuation add much less entropy than users think.
The comic's 1000 guesses/s online-attack assumption is optimistic; passwords should be sized for offline cracking of stolen hashes, which is far faster.

questions.query: How do ASLR and DEP work, and can they be bypassed?

key_points.text: ASLR randomly offsets the memory location of modules and certain in-memory structures so an attacker cannot predict addresses to jump to.
DEP marks certain memory regions, such as the stack, non-executable, so injected shellcode placed there cannot run.
Combined, ASLR and DEP make exploiting vulnerabilities with shellcode or return-oriented programming (ROP) exceedingly difficult.
Without ASLR the stack is at the same address on every run, so a stack buffer overflow can overwrite the saved return address (EIP) with a known address of attacker-controlled data.

DEP can be enforced on older x86 CPUs without an NX bit by using segmentation: limiting the code segment (CS) so execution above a boundary raises an exception while those addresses stay readable/writable as data.

questions.query: Is exploit-free software possible?

key_points.text: Software is too complex: huge codebases built on layers of libraries, OS functions and decades-old standards exceed what any one person can fully understand, so vulnerabilities remain.
Security knowledge gets lost over time in organizations as experienced developers move on, which is why old bug classes like SQL injection persist.
Developers are often taught insecure practices (e.g. building SQL queries by string concatenation) because security is neglected in education.
The seL4 microkernel was mathematically proven (2009, later extended to its ARM binary) to implement its specification exactly, including integrity and confidentiality properties.
Even a formal proof rests on assumptions: hand-written assembly, correct hardware, and hardware management such as cache and TLB handling are assumed, not proven.
Provably correct code still runs on hardware that may itself be exploitable (e.g. Meltdown and Spectre), so exploit-free software would require exploit-free hardware.

questions.query: Is it good secure programming practice to overwrite a sensitive variable before deleting it?

key_points.text: An optimizing compiler may remove a write to a variable that is never read again, so a naive overwrite/zeroing can be silently optimized away; use dedicated functions such as SecureZeroMemory.
Overwriting sensitive data once it is no longer needed is worthwhile because crash dumps, heap contents, hibernation images or memory dumps of running processes can expose it.
In garbage-collected languages with immutable strings (e.g. C#), reassigning a variable does not overwrite the old value, which lingers until collected.
Securing in-memory secrets also involves platform-specific measures: encrypting data in memory, pinning it to avoid paging, marking it read-only, and using APIs like .NET SecureString.
Physical remanence of overwritten RAM values is not a practical concern, so overwriting several times adds nothing; physical RAM attacks are rare and targeted.
The most important reason to clear stale data is defense against program bugs that expose uninitialized or stale memory, such as Heartbleed.

questions.query: How to avoid reverse engineering of an Android APK file

key_points.text: Completely preventing reverse engineering of an APK is impossible: an attacker can modify the app in any way and remove any protection; you can only make it harder.
Obfuscation with ProGuard (or the commercial DexGuard) slows reverse engineering, but obfuscated dex can still be disassembled to smali and understood by experienced reversers.
Move critical algorithms and secrets to a server-side service; never hardcode payment credentials, keys or tokens in the app, because they can be recovered even from obfuscated code.
Implementing sensitive parts natively with the NDK (.so libraries) makes them harder to decompile than Java/Dalvik bytecode.
Additional runtime defenses include encrypting parts of code/data, built-in checksums to detect tampering, and detecting or killing attached debuggers.

Only tamper-resistant hardware raises the bar substantially; security-sensitive logic should not depend on obscurity, and payments should rely on user credentials with end-to-end authentication rather than trusting the app.

questions.query: How secure are virtual machines really? Can malware in a VM affect the host?

key_points.text: VMs can definitely be crossed: networked VMs are reachable by worms and network-borne malware like any machine, so a VM needs the same security layers as a bare-metal system.
Even without overt communication, malware in co-located VMs can set up covert channels, e.g. timing channels through a shared CPU.
Rushby's 1981 separation-kernel work says isolation equivalent to physical separation requires that no stateful resource be shared between VMs, which x86 and practical systems cannot fully provide.
Hardware vulnerabilities such as Meltdown, Spectre, Foreshadow and ZombieLoad show that VM isolation can always leak.
Guest-to-host escapes exist, often through VM tools / guest-host integration and emulated devices; the Cloudburst exploit achieved code execution on VMware Workstation and ESX hosts.
Some malware detects that it is running in a VM and changes its behavior, frustrating analysts who use VMs to study it.

questions.query: How do the Meltdown and Spectre attacks work?

key_points.text: Speculative execution is a CPU optimization: using branch prediction, value prediction or prefetching, instructions are executed ahead of time and out of order, and rolled back if the prediction was wrong.

Meltdown exploits out-of-order memory reads so a user-space process can read kernel memory it should not access; Spectre manipulates branch prediction and allows cross- or intra-process memory disclosure.
Both rely on a cache side channel: measuring timing differences when accessing memory blocks to infer the secret value left in the cache.
Meltdown is easier to exploit than Spectre and has a known software mitigation (kernel page-table isolation, KPTI/KAISER).
Spectre works by coercing the branch predictor to speculatively execute instructions the program would not normally execute.

questions.query: Service orchestration vs choreography: differences and trade-offs

key_points.text: Orchestration is a single centralized executable business process (the orchestrator) that invokes and combines the participating services; choreography is a decentralized description of the collaboration defined by message exchanges and interaction rules between participants, so the two differ in where the control logic resides.

In orchestration the participating services do not know they are part of a larger composition (only the coordinator does); in choreography each participant knows when to execute its operations and with whom to interact.

Orchestration's advantages are reliability and control: central coordination with built-in error handling and transaction management (compensating transactions, alternative paths on faults) and better process visibility/modifiability.
Choreography's advantages are performance (no orchestration-layer overhead) and cost (no extra middleware); an orchestrator without high availability can become a single point of failure.
A BPEL process is a typical orchestration; event-driven processing, where agents react to events with no central logic, is a typical choreography.

questions.query: Why is it bad to read data directly from a database owned by a different microservice

key_points.text: A microservice's API is its contract while its database schema is an internal implementation detail; reading another service's database adds a dependency on that schema so the owning team can no longer change or replace it without breaking you.

Databases are poor at information hiding/encapsulation; keeping data behind a small API lets the owner reimplement storage (denormalize, switch to a document or graph store, add caching) transparently.
Direct reads put unwanted, unpredictable load on the other service's internals and tie your service's performance to their database.
The schema may contain internal-state details that do not represent the resources you care about, and write access would let you corrupt the other service's state without it knowing.
Through an API the providing team only has to keep the API backwards compatible; other teams querying its database couple its development to their schedules and domains.

questions.query: What is the dependency inversion principle and why is it important

key_points.text: DIP: high-level modules should not depend on low-level modules, both should depend on abstractions; abstractions should not depend on details, details should depend on abstractions.

The inversion is one of ownership: the high-level component owns the interface describing what it needs and low-level components implement it; merely putting an interface in front of a dependency does not invert the relationship.
Depending on a stable abstraction instead of an implementation reduces coupling and the need for changes at call sites, and allows choosing the implementation at run time.

Its main value is reuse: libraries that need infrastructure (e.g. logging) without forcing sub-dependencies on consumers, and business logic isolated from changing implementation details such as persistence or messaging libraries.
In a layered architecture, instead of business logic depending on the data access layer, the business layer depends on abstractions that the lower layer implements.
Limitations: part of the principle addressed C++ header coupling and matters less in Java/C#, and creating abstractions for components that will not be reused is over-engineering.

questions.query: Transactions across REST microservices: 2PC, sagas, or eventual consistency

key_points.text: Distributed (2PC) transactions spanning stateless REST services are a poor fit: 2PC needs comprehensive failure-recovery machinery and is still not fail-proof, leaving some transactions unable to complete and requiring manual repair.
Sagas/compensating transactions undo completed steps with compensating operations, at the cost of implementing compensations and a coordination mechanism, and compensation is also not fail-proof.

Eventual consistency is often better than occasional inconsistency: e.g. enqueue a NewUser message for a consumer that does the work in one local transaction, or keep each transaction inside one service and publish an event (USER_CREATED) that the other service reacts to.
If a synchronous, consistent result is required, remodel the services so the data that must be consistent (user and wallet) lives in the same service/database, moving closer to a monolith.

The 'Starbucks' model avoids two-phase commit: proceed best-effort and compensate on error, make services idempotent (re-callable with a task id) and return undo receipts, with a manual-handling queue as last resort.

questions.query: Message-driven vs event-driven approaches to application integration

key_points.text: Messages are directed to a specific addressable recipient, whereas an event is a signal that something happened, emitted for zero to many observers to react to.
Message-driven systems focus on addressable recipients that wait for messages; event-driven systems attach listeners to addressable event sources; a message can carry an encoded event as its payload.

Example: message-driven, the Order service sends an authorization request to Payment and gets a result; event-driven, Order publishes NewOrder, Payment subscribes and publishes AuthorizationAccepted/Declined events.
Event-driven lets other services subscribe to the same events (e.g. reporting), but the system becomes harder to understand and changing or removing events can break unknown subscribers.

There is no sharp distinction: messaging middleware (MOM/pub-sub bus) is the plumbing on which an event-driven architecture is built, and events can also be delivered without messaging, e.g. in-process callbacks.

questions.query: Difference between static class and singleton pattern

key_points.text: A singleton can implement interfaces and derive from base classes, so it can be handled polymorphically as just another implementation; a static class cannot.
A singleton is an instance whose reference can be passed as a parameter and treated as a normal object (enabling dependency injection); a static class offers only static methods and cannot be passed.
A singleton can be initialized lazily (or asynchronously) on first request, while a static class is generally initialized when it is loaded.
Singletons are easier to unit test: wherever a singleton is passed in, a mock or stub can be substituted.
Static classes suit stateless groups of utility functions (e.g. Math); a singleton suits something that must hold state or manage single access to a resource.
Neither is inherently thread-unsafe; both should usually be implemented to be thread-safe.
Static methods are bound at compile time, giving static classes a small performance advantage.

questions.query: What is a stack trace, and how can I use it to debug my application errors?

key_points.text: A stack trace is the list of method calls (the call stack) the application was in the middle of when an exception was thrown, showing not only where the error happened but how the program got there.
To locate the error, find the topmost 'at' line that belongs to your own application and inspect that file and line number.
With chained exceptions, look at the 'Caused by' sections; the root cause is usually the lowest 'Caused by' section.
If the root-cause frames are all library code, move up to the preceding 'Caused by' block and find the first frame originating from your code (e.g. your package).
Fix the cause where possible; when an exception cannot be prevented, catch only the specific exception you can handle, not a broad catch (Exception e).

questions.query: What is the difference between DAO and Repository patterns?

key_points.text: A DAO is an abstraction of data persistence, closer to the database and often table-centric; a Repository is an abstraction of a collection of objects, closer to the domain and dealing only in aggregate roots.
A Repository can be implemented using DAOs, but not the other way round.
A Repository is a narrower interface (Get(id), Find(spec), Add); an Update method belongs on a DAO, while with a Repository entity changes are tracked by a separate Unit of Work.
Both are ways of implementing a data access layer; the essence of the Repository pattern is that, to clients, it behaves like a collection (add, remove, contains).
A Repository usually handles one type of object and speaks domain-model terms, whereas a DAO may locate and store several related object types.
Some argue the distinction is semantic: a DAO's purpose is to hide data-access details, and a 'repository' is essentially good DAO design.

questions.query: Should I write small functions or put everything in one big loop?

key_points.text: A well-named small function makes it unnecessary to read its body; the name reveals intent better than the code itself, which is why the long-function approach must fall back on comments.
Replacing a comment with a well-named function turns the comment into testable code instead of a comment that can go stale.
A 300-line function may be faster to scan but is hard to truly read, since that requires executing it in your head; long uninterrupted blocks are maintenance nightmares and error-prone.
Extracting a helper is worthwhile when it isolates a self-contained piece of complexity; every call adds cognitive overhead, so tiny single-use functions can add more complexity than they remove.
The deeper problem in the example is a debug/test branch in production code; inject the test data (e.g. dependency injection of headers) so production code is tested as-is.
Line count alone is not a useful measure: long, trivial sequential code (e.g. setup/configuration) can be simple, while short nested logic can be hard to follow.

questions.query: What is the meaning of the 90/10 rule of program optimization?

key_points.text: Some code executes far more often than other code: loops and frequently taken branches run many times, while error handling or startup code runs once or never.
Some code takes much longer than other code, e.g. a database query or network fetch versus millions of arithmetic operations.
The 90/10 (or 80/20, Pareto) rule is a rule of thumb, not literally true; the exact numbers vary by program.
If a program must be faster, only a small number of lines matter; identifying the slow parts is often the biggest part of optimisation.
Much code is not worth optimising even if simplistic; the right algorithm is one that works and runs fast enough.
Changes that make code longer and more complex can still be a performance win, e.g. adding logic to avoid a single database call.

questions.query: Should an e-commerce application reserve products before attempting payment?

key_points.text: It is a hybrid business, user-experience and IT-capability problem; business should decide, but only after dialogue with IT about what is possible.
Real-time reservation requires the online ordering system to be connected to the back-end stock management system.
For generic software, offer both approaches as a configuration option and make reservation the default.
Charging the customer and then reporting the product out of stock is a poor experience, and refunding/undoing the transaction may incur fees for the retailer.
Put a hold on the product when it is ordered, like a shopping cart; abandoned holds are released after a timeout, and stale holds are re-checked for stock.
Payment processors separate authorisation from charging: authorise before reserving, and charge immediately, after a delay, or manually before shipping physical goods.

questions.query: How do I protect Python code from being read by users

key_points.text: No technical method can fully protect code against reverse engineering; even compiled programs and encrypted firmware have been reverse engineered.
Python is byte-code compiled and its byte-codes and exe-packager layouts are well understood, so it is very difficult to lock down.
Rely on legal and commercial means (licenses, contracts, terms and conditions), which work even when customers can read the code.
If the license check must be enforced, move it (or critical startup code) into a small native C extension, making it harder but not impossible to reverse engineer.
Compile Python to C with tools like Cython or Nuitka and ship binary extension modules so no Python byte code is left.
Offering the software as a hosted web service keeps the code and license checks on servers you control; a service cannot be copied.
Some open-source licenses of bundled components prohibit concealing their source or origins.

questions.query: What do you do when code review is just too hard (changes to complex fragile code)

key_points.text: A risky change to complex, fragile code is the last code to review less; review being too hard signals structural technical-debt problems to fix rather than work around.
Reduce complexity and fragility incrementally: extract units with well-defined behaviour, write tests for them, and refactor carefully under review.
Make a series of small, targeted changes each of which can be seen to be correct; a reviewer can send a broad change back to be split into smaller changesets.
Make fragile code find bugs: add assertions and debugging logic, run a slow but obviously correct implementation alongside in debug builds, and force rare situations to occur.
A solid automated test suite complements peer review rather than replacing it; full review also spreads understanding of the fragile code across the team.
Code review is not primarily for correctness; the author should ensure the change works, including non-regression, before submitting it for review.
Without understanding every detail a reviewer can still check smells, standards and tactical issues, assess risk areas, and ask that those risk areas be unit tested.

questions.query: Why would teams use the Fibonacci sequence for story points

key_points.text: The larger a story, the more uncertainty and the less accurate the estimate; a Fibonacci-like scale recognises this by deliberately reducing precision instead of producing falsely confident estimates.
Teams also use other non-linear scales such as powers of two, 1-2-5-8-20, or a modified sequence 0, 0.5, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 20, 40, 100 and '?'.
Widely spaced buckets make decisions easier: it is easier to say a story is more an 8 than a 5 than to choose between 7 and 8, and the gaps force a choice of bucket.
Stories estimated above about 20 are too big to estimate accurately and should be split; '?' signals the story is not understood or needs more information.
Because estimates are relative (20 is four times 5), larger intervals make differences in magnitude visible and provoke discussion when estimates diverge.

questions.query: How do I prevent Scrum from turning great developers into average developers

key_points.text: A daily meeting where developers report ticket completion to a manager is not Scrum but a well-known anti-pattern; the Daily Scrum is for team members to coordinate, not report.
Scrum depends on forming a self-organizing team that agrees on its goal and definition of done and strives for it together, not on individuals closing tickets.

Per the Scrum Guide the Daily Scrum is a 15-minute internal event whose structure the Development Team sets; the Scrum Master keeps outsiders from disrupting it, since self-organizing teams choose how best to do their work.

Turning the daily scrum into a ticket-count competition, or using Scrum to drive more output, causes the low-hanging-fruit behaviour; the sprint goal should be a business outcome, not an amount of work.
Done well, cross-functional teams, planning involvement, short release cycles and retrospectives help strong developers raise technical concerns, mentor, and improve architecture early.
Giving developers ownership makes them care about code quality and architecture; when nothing is theirs they stop caring.

questions.query: How to check your own proofs for mistakes (shoot down your proofs)

key_points.text: By analogy with code smells, collect 'proof smells' - symptoms like 'clearly' or 'obviously' that may hide a problem - and check for them when rereading.
Other proof smells include citing the proof of a previous result instead of the result itself and flippant use of a result with many technical preconditions.
Lamport's structured proof style (How to Write a Proof, and the 21st-century version) makes errors straightforward to detect and shows which assumptions and theorems each part uses.

Throw things at the proof: check it collapses when a necessary assumption is removed or it is applied outside its scope, and test generalizations and specializations, e.g. using Polya's How to Solve It heuristics.
Come up with multiple independent proofs, so the main result can be trusted even if one proof has a mistake in its details.

questions.query: Why does OAuth 2 have both access tokens and refresh tokens instead of one long-lived access token?

key_points.text: Short-lived self-contained (signed) access tokens can be validated by the resource server without a database lookup, while revocation is achieved by revoking the database-backed refresh token and not issuing new access tokens; this keeps revocation possible while scaling and avoiding a token-database single point of failure.

If an access token is compromised its short lifetime limits the attacker's window of abuse; a stolen refresh token alone is useless because exchanging it also requires the client id and client secret.

The trade-offs are a window during which access is revoked but an already-issued access token is still valid, and more complex client logic (on an invalid access token, try the refresh flow, retry the request, else re-authenticate).

The access token is sent on every request to resource servers, whereas the refresh token is sent only to the authorization server (a different audience), so it is exposed far less often and resource servers never see it (compartmentalization).
Refresh tokens can be rotated: each refresh returns a new refresh token and invalidates the old one, which reduces the threat from a leaked refresh token.
Each refresh is a checkpoint where the server can re-evaluate the client (e.g. IP change, request frequency, adaptive access checks) and refuse the refresh, forcing the user to re-authenticate.

questions.query: How is OAuth 2 different from OAuth 1?

key_points.text: OAuth 2 delegates security to the HTTPS/TLS transport, whereas OAuth 1 is transport-independent and protects requests itself with its own security mechanisms.

OAuth 1.0 requires the client to compute a signature (HMAC-SHA1 with a shared secret or RSA-SHA1) over each API call using two credentials, which is complicated to implement; OAuth 2.0 needs no signatures on API calls and uses a single token.

OAuth 1.0's security rests on the client keeping its secret key confidential, so it effectively only supports confidential clients; OAuth 2.0 (RFC 6749) adds public clients such as smartphone apps that cannot keep a secret.

OAuth 2's lead author (Eran Hammer) argued it is less secure because bearer tokens offer no security beyond SSL/TLS: clients that skip certificate verification or typos such as http instead of https void the token's security, and the spec is more complex and less interoperable.
Providers such as Facebook and Google implement slightly different versions of OAuth 2, so it is less uniform across platforms than OAuth 1.
RFC 6749 addresses open redirectors while RFC 5849 does not, so OAuth 1.0's oauth_callback parameter can be a security hole; with a confidential client there is no practical security difference.

questions.query: What's the difference between ISO 8601 and RFC 3339 date formats?

key_points.text: RFC 3339 is (mostly) a profile of ISO 8601 for Internet timestamps that specifies a complete date and time representation, with only fractional seconds optional.
RFC 3339 requires four-digit years (no truncated two-digit years) and allows only a period as the decimal point for fractional seconds.
RFC 3339 allows the 'T' separator to be replaced by a space, which ISO 8601 does not allow (ISO only allows omitting it by mutual agreement).

Neither is a superset of the other: RFC 3339 allows a '-00:00' offset (borrowed from RFC 2822) that ISO 8601 forbids, while ISO 8601 allows forms RFC 3339 rejects, such as the basic format without hyphens and colons (20201209T160953Z) and ordinal dates (2020-344).
A safe strategy is to generate date-time strings valid under both standards and to use an existing standard library for parsing and formatting.

questions.query: Security auditor demands plain-text passwords, password history and SSH private keys for PCI audit: how to respond?

key_points.text: Do not comply: producing plain-text passwords and private keys is dangerous, and releasing them would itself violate the PCI standard (and other standards); escalate to management/legal counsel and the auditor's QSA company or card brand.
Passwords are stored as one-way hashes (e.g. in LDAP), so plain-text passwords cannot be provided short of brute-forcing the hashes.

Legitimate audits examine controls and processes, not credentials: they review password-strength and hashing algorithms (that hashes cannot be reversed), password-history reuse prevention, and run authorised penetration tests; auditors have no need for information that gives them access to systems.

Answer from policy and evidence: show usernames and recent password-change times rather than passwords, explain what is and is not logged and provide what is available, and ask whether logging needs improving.
Never fake or falsify records such as six months of password changes or file transfers.
The request may itself be a social-engineering test, and handing over credentials and keys would let the holder impersonate users and commit fraud undetected.

questions.query: What are the different widely used RAID levels and when should I consider them?

key_points.text: RAID performance comes from striping (spreading data across disks so all disks' IO queues are used at once); redundancy comes from mirroring or from parity stripes that can recreate lost data after a hardware failure.
Each RAID configuration is biased toward performance or toward redundancy, and choosing a level depends on its advantages and its hardware requirements such as the number of drives.
RAID levels like 0, 1 and 5 do not ensure data integrity: a corrupted file is mirrored or paritied and committed to disk anyway, whereas RAID-Z claims file-level integrity.
On direct-attached storage RAID can be implemented at two layers: hardware or software.

questions.query: Is TRIM needed for SSDs in RAID, and how do SSD garbage collection and over-provisioning behave in RAID arrays?

key_points.text: TRIM is mostly unnecessary on modern SSDs if enough spare space (~20%) is reserved; enterprise drives have more spare area by default and firmware tuned for continuous use, giving good write consistency without trimming.
The drive's garbage collector works inside the drive and knows nothing about the outside environment, so it is mostly unaffected by the array's RAID level.
Parity-based RAID levels can in some implementations increase the write amplification factor, meaning more work for the drive's GC routines.
SLC has largely left the enterprise; flash grades are distinguished by rated rewrite cycles (about 25-30k for HMLC/MLCe, 5-10k for 3D MLC, about 3k for planar MLC and 3D TLC).

questions.query: What does thin pool mean in Docker (thin provisioning)?

key_points.text: A thin pool is the backing storage source used by thin provisioning: it allocates storage on demand, much like virtual memory gives every process a full address space.

Fat/thick provisioning reserves the full claimed physical space up front even if little is used; thin provisioning lets a user claim more space than is physically reserved (over-allocation, like RAM over-commit).
A thin pool has a metadata space storing pointers and a data space storing real data; no data chunk is actually allocated until a write request arrives.

Docker's devicemapper storage driver in direct-lvm mode builds the thin pool from block devices; container creation fails when free data or metadata space falls below the Thin Pool Minimum Free Space, requiring more storage or removing unused images.

questions.query: Technical details of Windows Server 2012 data deduplication: algorithms, chunking, comparison with ZFS dedup

key_points.text: Server 2012 deduplication is built on the VSS subsystem, which explains its asynchronous (post-process) nature.
Deduplicated chunks live in a chunk store; backup software with dedupe support backs up only the much smaller dedupe store, otherwise backups stay full size.
A 2011 Microsoft research paper at USENIX FAST'11 on practical deduplication, including deduplication in primary storage, likely informed the design.
The canonical algorithm for variable-sized content-defined blocks is Rabin fingerprints.

questions.query: How can I extend the life of my Raspberry Pi SD card?

key_points.text: SD cards use wear-leveling, so using a card much bigger than needed (plenty of free space) spreads writes over more blocks and can more than proportionally extend its life.
Wear leveling matters because file systems like FAT hammer the same sectors over and over.
SD cards do not report bad data with an I/O error the way hard drives do, so file system choice matters for reliable storage.
Do not swap on the SD card; use compressed RAM swap (zram) instead.
Move write-heavy directories such as /var/log (and database dirs) off the card, to network storage or to RAM-backed tmpfs.
Run a RAM-resident system that loads the storage image into RAM at boot and flushes changes back to storage only periodically.

questions.query: What's the difference between faking, mocking, and stubbing in unit tests?

key_points.text: A fake has a working implementation that takes a shortcut making it unsuitable for production (e.g. an in-memory database).
A stub provides canned/predefined answers to calls made during the test.
A mock is pre-programmed with expectations that form a specification of the calls it is expected to receive; it is used for behaviour verification.
The stub/mock distinction lies in usage: the test asserts against a mock, never against a stub; the same fake object can act as either.
'Test double' is the general term covering stubs, mocks and fakes (informally all are often called mocks).
Per Fowler, stubs support state verification while mocks support behaviour verification.

questions.query: How should I unit test multithreaded code?

key_points.text: Separate core logic from thread-handling code (Humble Object pattern from xUnit Test Patterns) so the logic can be tested synchronously and reproducibly; the thin threading wrapper needs few tests.
Bugs in multithreaded code are probabilistic; timing-dependent race conditions cannot be tested repeatably, so tests should instead verify that the locking strategy lets threads interact as intended.
Order thread interactions in tests with timing delays rather than external synchronization (which would mask bugs), tuning delays to avoid fragile tests.
There are infinitely many thread interleavings; write highly concurrent stress tests that check invariants, or use deterministic-interleaving frameworks that force specific interleavings.
Tools help: ConTest instruments code with sleeps/yields to vary interleavings, plus static analysis (FindBugs), model checkers (Java PathFinder, SPIN) and MultithreadedTC.
Always give concurrency tests a timeout because broken ones can hang, and relay exceptions from worker threads back to the test thread.
Fuzz testing samples behaviour randomly and can find bugs, but is not an assurance of correctness.

questions.query: What is the difference between integration and unit tests?

key_points.text: A unit test isolates the class under test by mocking its dependencies; an integration test uses the real collaborators to check that modules work together.
A green unit test relies on the (often wrong) assumption that the rest of the software works; integration tests exercise code close to reality and show whether a feature actually works.
Integration tests verify that the assumptions about interactions encoded in the unit tests' mocks were correct.
Both are needed for risk reduction: unit tests cannot test interactions between modules, while integration tests exercise each module's functionality only to a small degree.
Integration tests touching databases or remote systems are slower, run less often, and their failures are harder to localize; integration tests may still stub some dependencies.
What counts as a 'unit' is context dependent, so the unit/integration boundary is a movable line.
Crossing physical layers (I/O plus content, a real service call) makes a test an integration test.

questions.query: Is mutation testing useful in practice compared with code coverage?

key_points.text: 100% code coverage does not mean the code is 100% tested; coverage only shows what code was executed.
Mutation testing generates mutants and checks that the tests detect them, giving more confidence in the test suite.
Tests can exercise the application correctly yet lack checkpoints that verify results; mutation-style checks expose such faulty or incomplete tests.
A simpler variant mutates the baseline data instead of the code and reruns the tests; any test that still passes is faulty or incomplete.

questions.query: How to determine code coverage of basic blocks when fuzzing a binary

key_points.text: Correct disassembly of an executable is undecidable in general (related to the halting problem), so extracting all basic blocks of a binary is very difficult.
Best-effort coverage can be approached by combining concrete and symbolic exploration of the program (concolic / dynamic symbolic execution).
Microsoft Research's SAGE (Patrice Godefroid) implements this approach.
Godefroid's idea underlies many other tools, such as KLEE, Mayhem, and Pin-based concolic execution with Z3.

questions.query: How does the SQL injection from the Bobby Tables XKCD comic work?

key_points.text: The program builds the SQL by concatenating user input into the query; the ' in the name is a string delimiter that closes the literal early, not a comment.
The ; terminates the original statement so a second injected statement (DROP TABLE Students) is executed.
The -- comments out the rest of the original query so the result is still valid SQL; injection only works when the resulting SQL is valid.
The correct defence is parameterized queries / prepared statements (bind parameters), not sanitizing inputs.
Many frameworks disallow multiple statements per query, but injection still works without a second statement, e.g. ' OR '1'='1 to bypass a login check.

questions.query: Should the OK button be on the left or right of the Cancel button?

key_points.text: Follow the platform's UI guidelines rather than sub-optimizing one dialog: Windows puts OK before Cancel (Cancel on the right), macOS puts the action button rightmost with Cancel to its left, Android puts the dismissive action on the left and the affirmative on the right.
For web apps, follow the platform most of your users are on (check server logs); absent that, the common guideline is OK first, Cancel last.
Label buttons with what they do instead of a generic OK; an explicit label acts as just-in-time help and gives users confidence.
Make the most commonly chosen button the highlighted default, except when its action is dangerous, so users cannot trigger it accidentally with Enter.
A left-to-right reading/progression metaphor argues for Cancel (a step back) on the left and OK (a step forward) on the right.
Visually emphasize the primary action over the secondary one and place it to follow the form's path to completion (Wroblewski's primary/secondary actions).

questions.query: What is aria-label and how should I use it?

key_points.text: aria-label lets assistive technology such as screen readers attach a label to an otherwise anonymous element, like <label> does, for cases where an on-screen label is impractical, e.g. a close button showing only 'X'.

aria-label has no effect in ordinary browsers for sighted users, so it does not help non-screen-reader users (e.g. people with intellectual disabilities) understand an ambiguous 'X'; the title attribute is still needed for them.
Use both title and aria-label to serve different users; aria-label can carry screen-reader-specific context (e.g. 'Back to the page') while title says 'Close'.
ARIA attributes bridge accessibility gaps native HTML cannot cover and change nothing visually.
aria-labelledby references visible element(s) by id and can combine several labels; aria-label supplies a label that is not displayed.
A title tooltip appears only on mouse hover, so it does not help keyboard-only users with mobility disabilities or users who cannot see it.

questions.query: How can I find an optimum set of distinguishable colors for 10 players?

key_points.text: For a fixed count, generate equidistant hue values in HSV space (hue = i/n with fixed saturation and value).

Stepping hue by the golden ratio conjugate (fmod(i*0.618..., 1)) gives a good spread for any number of players, a property of the equidistribution theorem; the golden ratio is proven best among irrationals.

HSV hue is not perceptually uniform (orange is a thin slice, green a wide one), so equal hue steps yield near-identical greens; a correction curve from a perceptual metric such as CIEDE2000 improves the result.
Prefer familiar, nameable colors (StarCraft/Warcraft player palettes, basic Crayola names) because players must talk about and refer to the colors.
Do not rely on color alone: add symbols, shapes or hatch patterns (and hover/labels) so colorblind players, who may not distinguish red and green, can tell sides apart.
Ten distinguishable colors is very hard; charts solve the same problem by combining a few colors with a few shapes or patterns (e.g. 4 colors x 4 shapes = 16 markers).
The 16 ANSI terminal colors, spread over the corners and edges of the RGB cube, are a ready-made standard set to pick from.

questions.query: Is the hierarchical folder structure dying in favour of search, tags and metadata?

key_points.text: Hierarchical folders are not dying but are being complemented: the key trend is decoupling views from the underlying file system, so one store supports many views (search, tags, folders).
Historically file UX mirrored the OS's abstracted hierarchical path/file model, which programming languages also use for file access.

Manual folder management is becoming a power-user niche: people will not pay the large upfront cost of organizing for a small future retrieval benefit, and full-system search and tagging mean typical users need not care where files live.
Categorization still matters, but apps increasingly do it automatically (photos grouped by date or location) instead of making users file manually.

Search finds known items but does not help explore what you have; specialized apps (music by artist/album) and folders remain useful, especially for shared, heterogeneous assets no single app manages.
A hierarchy forces storing an item under one chosen attribute order (Red/Square vs Square/Red); attribute-based retrieval lets users find items by any attributes in any order.

questions.query: How to discover what users need and not what they want?

key_points.text: Focus on goals: ask what users need to achieve, not what functionality or form they want.
Ask how they currently achieve the goal and what makes current methods difficult; research problems, not solutions.
Research needs independently of your own ideas: reactions to something you built reveal wants, not needs; ask about their day, context of use and how they think about their tools.
Immerse in the users' world (on-site observation, notes, talking to users and customers) because users satisfied with incremental improvements cannot imagine how things could be better.
Understand users well enough to put yourself in their shoes, and be honest about flaky requirements: users often do not know what is possible, so innovation comes from the designer, not the users.
Remove things from your solution until it no longer solves the problem: wants are accessories, needs are the core.

questions.query: Is there a CSS parent selector?

key_points.text: Selectors Level 4 adds the :has() pseudo-class, which selects a parent based on its descendants, e.g. li:has(> a.active).
CSS 2 has no parent selector; the workaround is to put the class on the li (parent) instead of the a, or use JavaScript.

A parent selector was long withheld because it is expensive: the browser must examine an element's descendants (potentially waiting until the document is parsed) before it can decide the parent's style.
:has() is not limited to parent selection: it can match on siblings (span:has(+ div)) and combine with :not() (div:not(:has(p))).
The :focus-within pseudo-class selects a parent when one of its descendants has focus.

questions.query: What exactly is RESTful programming?

key_points.text: Hypermedia as the engine of application state (HATEOAS): the client needs no prior knowledge of the API's structure; the server supplies the locations and actions through hypermedia links, and this is the key differentiator of REST.
Per Fielding, a REST API should spend almost all of its descriptive effort defining the media types used for representing resources and driving application state.
Resources are identified by URIs and manipulated through a common set of verbs (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE mapping to CRUD) rather than action-specific URLs.
GET must never modify state and should be idempotent, which is what makes it cacheable; non-idempotent operations such as add-to-cart use POST.
REST relies on stateless, cacheable client-server communication; representations declare how they may be cached (Cache-Control), which is the most consequential property.
REST is an architectural style defined by Roy Fielding in his dissertation, describing the architecture of the web; it is not tied to HTTP.

questions.query: Understanding unique keys for array children in React

key_points.text: React uses the key prop to identify which element corresponds to which DOM node during reconciliation, so it can make minimal DOM changes instead of re-rendering everything.
A key must be unique among its siblings and static (unchanged) across renders; it is about identity, not merely performance.
Using the array index as the key is an anti-pattern when items are inserted or reordered: React may mix up elements and mutate the wrong one.
Every child produced from an array, including elements nested inside the mapped children, needs a key; otherwise React warns and may re-render the whole row.
The key is set where the array is rendered (in the parent), not inside the child component.

questions.query: When and how does a PWA update itself?

key_points.text: A PWA update is triggered only by a change in the linked manifest.json or by any byte change in the service worker script (e.g. bumping a version constant).
A newly detected service worker normally activates only on the next load, so two reloads are needed to see a change, although it can be made to activate immediately.
The HTTP cache expiry for the service worker and manifest must be very short or none; otherwise the browser will not see changes for days.
Without a service worker nothing is cached and the page loads fresh every time; the manifest only provides the home-screen icon and app-like launch.

With a service worker, the chosen caching strategy (cache falling back to network, network falling back to cache, cache then network) governs updates; precached files are refreshed in the background and shown on the next session or after prompting the user to refresh.
A network-first strategy avoids showing stale content on load but gives up the performance benefit of caching.

questions.query: Why not use double or float to represent currency?

key_points.text: Binary floating-point types cannot exactly represent most base-10 fractions such as 0.1 or 0.01 (of the cent values in [0,1] only 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75 and 1 are exact).
The small representation errors accumulate as more additions, subtractions, multiplications and divisions are performed.
Use an exact decimal type (BigDecimal, C# decimal) or integer counts of the smallest unit (int/long cents) for monetary amounts.
The issue is meeting human base-10 expectations: rounding boundary cases (e.g. 3.465 stored as 3.46499...) round the wrong way, rarely enough to escape casual testing.

Counterpoint: doubles can be acceptable with correct cent rounding and enough significant digits; the real danger is combining very large and very small values or summing unbounded amounts, as in accounting.
